#523. Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.

Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term "associate membership."

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.

Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.

"The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.

They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.

"Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.

"What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said.

Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.

"We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States."

He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.

But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.

"The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said.

Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues."

But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world.

He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace."

Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time."

"There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement."

Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges.

"It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said.

#522. Ancient Meteorite Found in the Sahara Holds Secrets About Mars’ Watery Past

In 2022, a strange rock was found in the Sahara Desert, and now a new analysis reveals that it’s even more valuable to science than it first appeared. This fragment, weighing about two pounds, came from Mars’ crust. It was likely ejected by an impact, flying through space until it eventually reached Earth. The rock is one of the oldest known samples from our neighboring planet, estimated to be at least 4.1 billion years old. At that time, Earth was a young planet with intense geological activity, likely with oceans but no animals, plants, or any other complex life.

The location is not what makes this finding surprising. The Sahara has long been a kind of natural archive of the history of Earth and the solar system. Among its sands, scientists have found 40-million-year-old fossils and other meteorites. In 2019, for example, a 4.5-billion-year-old fragment was recovered that, according to recent research, may have come from an ancient, now-vanished protoplanet, possibly as large as the moon.

The meteorite, named Teghaza 001, might have remained just another entry in the collection of Martian fragments found on Earth. Although these rocks are extraordinarily useful for studying Mars’ composition and geological history, they often provide limited information about the environmental conditions of its distant past. However, a series of studies published in the journals Science and Science Advances revealed that Teghaza 001 is not like other samples. In addition to being exceptionally old, it has preserved chemical traces of the interaction between materials in the Martian crust and its ancient hydrosphere.

“One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars,” Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory said in a press release.

Tiny crystals of a mineral called apatite preserves signatures of two sources of hydrogen: one originating from the interior of Mars and the other related to its ancient hydrosphere. In other words, the meteorite contains material that was altered by a water-rich environment. For years, there has been considerable evidence that Mars once harbored liquid water on its surface. Today, some of the big questions about the planet are whether that water allowed microscopic life to emerge and what happened to change this once hospitable environment.

This meteorite reveals that there was an exchange of materials between the magma deep within Mars and a watery surface. Since the rock comes from just about 500 million years after Mars and the rest of our solar system formed, this volatility occurred very early in the planet’s existence.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” added Lee Saper, another NASA scientist who contributed to the research. “It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water.”

Today, Mars is a cold and barren planet, but it was not always that way. Evidence gathered by space missions suggests that it once had rivers, lakes, and possibly large bodies of water. But how that transformation happened over billions of years has remained a mystery. Answering that question is part of the reasoning behind sending probes, rovers, and perhaps, one day, crewed missions to Mars. But sometimes science is about serendipity, and answers arrive in the form of extraordinarily unlikely meteorites.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

#519. Learn in context, speak with confidence — 1 year of Rosetta Stone Sapphire is just $127.20

#517. White Noise Machines Worthy of Your Nightstand in 2026: Snooz, Hatch, and More

I have chronic insomnia. I need a white noise machine, a sleep mask, a pitch-black room, and maybe some light tranquilizers just to fall asleep. (I'm joking, sort of.) If I'm traveling and forget my sound machine, I have to play white noise from my perpetually dying phone. Whether you're shopping for your kiddo or yourself, a white noise machine can help everyone sleep better at night.

These devices are simple, even as companies keep adding bells and whistles. They now come in all shapes and sizes, with options for playing different noise frequencies and soothing nature sounds—whether you need one at home or a portable model for life on the go. And they’re not just for kids or babies; if, like me, you want to quiet your inner monologue and finally drift off, this guide is for you.

We've tested everything: the best sleep trackers, sunrise alarm clocks, mattresses, and extreme alarm clocks. Check out all of the WIRED Reviews team's sleep coverage for our recommendations.

Note: If you're buying for a child or a baby, keep sound machines to no more than 50 decibels and farther than 200 centimeters (6.5 feet) from where they sleep.

“Colors” of noise are measured similarly to light. Pure white noise is a mix of all the frequencies humans can hear, so while these machines are often called “white noise" machines, white noise itself isn't always a relaxing sound (think of the static on your TV). Pink and brown noise are at the lower end of the spectrum, aren't as grating, and have been found to help people sleep a little more deeply. If you've seen pink noise, brown noise, and green noise amid all the white noise machine chatter, it's because, more often than not, you'll find those options bundled into one machine. If you think of sound waves as being loosely analogous to light waves, then the different colors of noise refer to different parts of the sound spectrum. The fun thing about using a sound machine for sleep is that you get to experiment with these noise frequencies to find what works best for you.

We're always on the lookout for new products to add to our Best Sunrise Alarm Clocks guide, and the Hatch Restore 3 definitely earned its place. It builds on earlier Hatch models—which we also tested and really enjoyed—with two additional buttons, bringing the total to four. That might not sound like a major change, but when you're sleepy and want to make a quick adjustment without reaching for the app, those extra buttons come in handy. During her testing, WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell found that this model's light wasn't as bright as in previous iterations and didn't quite deliver on the sound machine's “Sunlight” function. Still, it offers an extensive sound collection when you sign up for the subscription.

WIRED’s resident wearable tester, Boutayna Chokrane, tested this clock for her sleep trackers guide. (Read her full review here.) This brand-new white noise machine also doubles as a sunrise alarm clock and a passive sleep tracker. It uses motion-based tracking to monitor your sleep from your nightstand. The data focuses on the essentials—sleep duration and stages—and appears in interactive visuals. There are no cameras or microphones monitoring you as you sleep, and best of all, your data isn’t locked behind a Hatch+ membership. The machine also features adjustable volume, fade-out timers, customizable full-color light scenes, a gradual sunrise light to wake you gently, and a sunset wind-down light to help you prepare for bed. For sleep-inducing sounds, it offers white noise, nature sounds, sleep stories, and guided meditations. With a Hatch+ subscription, you'll also get access to more than 2,500 sounds, stories, and meditations to help lull you to sleep. Although it's the priciest option in this guide, it's a triple threat: a sunrise clock, a dimmable bedside light, and a sound machine.

The Snooz white noise machine focuses on one thing and one thing only: white noise. Its sound is generated by a real fan, not just fan sounds. There's no need to push extra buttons or fidget when you'd rather be falling asleep. Its design is simple, and there's no overthinking this device—it's insanely easy to use. Simply plug it in, press the power button, then twist the mesh sleeve to increase or decrease the volume. Note that it's also meant to be placed away from the bed in a more central position in the bedroom, rather than on a nightstand. This helps project the sound more evenly. —Julia Forbes

As Hatch phases out the older Hatch Rest, this kids' sound machine takes its place with a fresh look and an updated app interface, making it easier than ever to create routines for your kids. Reviewer Nena Farrell uses it with her son, who loves it—especially the easy-to-use nightlight button he can press himself. Unlike other Hatch sunrise clock models, this one doesn't offer gradual sunrises, but it does glow in fun colors and play music. You'll also get a three-month subscription to Hatch+ content.

This compact, portable sound machine is specifically designed for parents to take on the go. One side is the speaker, and the other is a night light. The night light isn't super bright, but it will help you navigate around a sleeping baby rather than using your phone’s flashlight. During testing, former WIRED reviewer Julia Forbes found that the included clip isn't the most flexible, but it allows for attachment to a stroller strap, diaper bag, purse, or backpack. You can choose from several options beyond white noise, and the sound is surprisingly strong and crisp for such a small machine. With Bluetooth connectivity, you can also stream your child's preferred sounds.

The Restnature sound machine is tiny—it would easily fit in a pocket. When a former WIRED reviewer tested it, she was impressed by its 16 diverse sound options, including birds, fire, and other nature sounds, lullabies, and different-color noises. There are convenient 30-, 60-, and 90-minute timer options, and it gets very loud—but the sound quality starts to suffer at the highest volume. The other portable players on this list offer more features, but this is still a solid choice if you need a machine that's as small as possible to take on the go. (Rechargeable with USB-C.)

I've had this basic white noise machine for over a decade, and it still works well. It has a DC power jack, but it can also be used cord-free with four AA batteries for portability. It's pretty basic, but it has everything most people are looking for in a sound machine. There's a knob to control volume and a button for 15-, 30-, or 60-minute timers (after which the machine will turn off). You can also choose between thunder, ocean waves, brook (which sounds like a bubbling river and running water), summer night (which sounds like wind, owl hoots, and chirping), rain, and classic white noise. The volume knob has worn a bit over a decade of use and needs to be set high to sound loud. It can also be finicky when used only on batteries and may suddenly die. However, since this thing is only $25 and has worked well for over a decade, I'm not too mad that it's showing some signs of age.

When I first get a sound machine, I note how clear the directions are, and the difficulty and time it takes to set up the gadget. I test each of these machines every night for at least one week of nightly testing (I often test them for longer).

During testing, I'm asking these questions and looking for these standard features:

Volume: Is it controlled with buttons or a knob? How easy is it to control the volume, especially when on my nightstand? I make sure to note how quiet and loud it is on each end of the spectrum.

Timers: Many folks like to turn off their sound machine after they've fallen asleep. Does the white noise machine offer preset timers, and if so, does it have several options to customize the time? Does it work accurately?

Sound options: This may be the biggest feature people are looking for. I tend to recommend white noise machines with various sounds, from white noise to nature noises, so that there's an option for every type of snoozer. I try to sleep with at least one sound per night during testing, and note if any have strange patterns. (Although I love the Homedics pick above, I tend to focus on the nature sounds, as its white noise option has an imperceptible beeping in the background that only I seem to hear.)

Other special features: Some of the best WIRED-tested sound machines on this list also double as a sleep tracker or sunrise alarm clock! If you have limited space or budget, it's ideal to get a machine that can do multiple things for you. Conversely, I love that the Snooz option above is analog and only uses a real fan machine to generate noise, so I note that for folks who want to pare down their number of bedside gadgets.

Can White Noise Machines Typically Run All Night?

If you plan on keeping your white noise machine playing sound on a loop all night, make sure first that it has the capacity to do so. Some machines run on 30-, 60-, or 90-minute timers that auto-shut off, while others are continuous.

Does a Fan Make a Good White Noise Machine?

In a pinch, a desk or box fan can stand in for a white noise machine. It provides steady noise to help you fall asleep and can also keep hot sleepers comfortable. But if you’d rather not cool the room or want a wider range of sounds, a sound machine is the better choice.

How Does WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?

WIRED’s product recommendations are chosen to serve readers, based on what's new, popular, and useful on the market. Although we receive a small cut of most sales when readers click to buy recommended products, revenue does not influence our choices. Samples are either provided by companies or purchased and expensed.

What Does WIRED Do With the Sound Machines After Testing Them?

Just like all products we test, some top picks are kept for long-term testing and comparison purposes, while everything is donated to our local communities when testing is finished.

#516. Heres how to track the Swift telescopes final hours before it crashes

NASA expects its Swift space telescope to re-enter Earth's atmosphere early Wednesday, ending over two decades of Swift's monitoring of sudden, powerful events in space.

The U.S. Space Force's prediction puts the re-entry at about 3:30 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 4. Most of the spacecraft should burn up as it falls through the atmosphere, though some pieces may reach the ground, according to NASA.

Though the agency doesn't offer a live orbital tracker of the spacecraft, you can monitor Swift's final days — or hours — through the agency's blog, as well as some third-party websites and apps.

Swift, whose official name is the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory,  will meet its demise after NASA and commercial contractor Katalyst Space tried to save it with a robotic spacecraft designed to boost it into a higher orbit. That $30 million rescue attempt failed, which means scientists have lost a quick-response telescope to study brief cosmic events. NASA says other missions will help fill some of the gap, but its absence will leave researchers with fewer ways to follow up on new discoveries.

"While deeply disappointed at the outcome, I'm nonetheless incredibly appreciative of the heroic efforts undertaken by the collective Katalyst and Swift teams," Brad Cenko, the mission's principal investigator, told Mashable in August. "I sincerely do view this effort as a success, even if we were not able to reach our ultimate goal."

To follow Swift's descent, you can read NASA's posts at https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift. NASA and the Space Force will continue updating the re-entry predictions, as the timing and location could shift.

But if you want a live look at its whereabouts, several websites provide global mapping and visualization tools for satellites like Swift, using its unique catalog designation, NORAD ID 28485. The data directly comes from the Space Force, which tracks satellites.

Visual trackers, such as Orbital Radar, N2YO, and KeepTrack, take this mathematical information from Space-Track.org, the public portal operated by the U.S. military, and plug it into their own map engines.

NASA launched Swift in 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts: flashes of high-energy light produced by some of the universe's most powerful explosions. Swift could spot a burst and quickly turn toward it to observe the fading light. It also helped scientists study objects like black holes and stars that flare in X-rays.

Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable's Light Speed newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

Earth's upper atmosphere creates drag on satellites in low orbit, slowing them and pulling them down. Recent solar activity increased that effect on Swift. NASA hired Katalyst to build a spacecraft that could approach the observatory, grab it, and raise its orbit. But ongoing control problems with the servicing spacecraft, LINK, ended the plan before it could attempt the capture and boost maneuvers.

Swift briefly returned to science observations after the unsuccessful rescue mission. It homed in on hundreds of targets, including the remains of stellar explosions, active black holes in distant galaxies, and comets in our solar system. On Oct. 20, Swift reached an altitude of 171 miles and could no longer counter the drag. The spacecraft entered a protective mode, and its operations team sent a command to end the mission.

NASA says surviving fragments could fall anywhere between 20.6 degrees south and 20.6 degrees north latitude. That band stretches around the world near the equator. The chance of someone on Earth being harmed by debris is "unlikely," with a chance of about 1 in 2,100, according to the agency.

Elisha Sauers writes about space for Mashable, taking deep dives into NASA's moon and Mars missions, chatting up astronauts and history-making discoverers, and jetting above the clouds. Through 17 years of reporting, she's covered a variety of topics, including health, business, and government, with a penchant for public records requests. She previously worked for The Virginian-Pilot in Norfolk, Virginia, and The Capital in Annapolis, Maryland. Her work has earned numerous state awards, including the Virginia Press Association's top honor, Best in Show, and national recognition for narrative storytelling. For each year she has covered space, Sauers has won National Headliner Awards, including first place for her Sex in Space series. Send space tips and story ideas to [email protected] or text 443-684-2489. Follow her on X at @elishasauers.

#515. Dating over 40? You have better things to do than swipe on the wrong apps.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Dating over 40 doesn’t mean you need an app with “senior” in the name or a profile that reads like a marriage application. Maybe you’re dating after divorce, fitting first dates around a custody schedule, or ready to meet someone new after time on your own. You might want a long-term relationship, a casual connection, or a reason to put on something other than your work-from-home pants. You don’t have to be looking for the same thing as everyone else, but it helps to know which apps suit what you want.

Hinge is my top pick among the best dating apps for over 40, particularly if you want a relationship and appreciate a profile that gives you something to talk about. Match is worth comparing if you prefer more detailed profiles, while Tinder is an option for exploring something casual. But the best choice also depends on who’s using it near you, what you can do for free, and whether the experience makes you want to meet someone or throw your phone into the sea.

There’s reason to be hopeful without pretending the apps are magic. In a 2026 SSRS survey, half of U.S. adults who had ever used a dating site or app said they’d been in a committed relationship with someone they met through one. The goal, of course, is to spend less time evaluating profiles and more time figuring out whether you enjoy someone’s company. The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections Tinder — top pick for fast hookups Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups Pure — best for anonymous hookups OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

“I wouldn’t let more than a few days go by before transitioning to an in-person meeting or at least a video call,” Suzannah Weiss, sex/couples therapist and resident sexologist for Erojoy, tells Mashable.

Hinge is my pick for the best dating app for people over 40 who want a relationship and a little more to go on than someone’s best vacation photo. You can like a specific photo or prompt answer and attach a comment, giving you a way to start a conversation about something you noticed. Matching and chatting are free, though you’re limited in how many likes you can send each day.

Your questionable karaoke choices, the hobby you’ve taken up, or what makes a weekend feel well spent can all give someone a reason to reach out. If you’re returning to dating after a long relationship, prompts help you decide what to share without having to explain your entire life story.

I picked Hinge because its profile format gives you something useful to work with before you match. A thoughtful answer can reveal a shared interest, a difference in priorities, or an easy opening question.

“Comment on something in the person’s profile, like an activity they’re doing in their photos or an interest listed in their bio,” Weiss tells Mashable. “This will make your message stand out amid the generic ones.”

If writing about yourself feels awkward, Hinge’s “Your World” prompts, developed with psychotherapist Esther Perel, offer prompts like “I’m in my element when…” and “I could stay up all night talking about…”

"Match Note" is a useful feature for sharing more personal information you want potential matches to know without putting it on your public profile. You might use it to explain that you’re sober, recently out of a relationship, or looking for non-monogamy. The note is shared when there’s mutual interest, and the other person has to acknowledge it before moving forward. (So they can't later say, "I didn't know.")

For opening-message nerves, Hinge's optional "Convo Starters" suggests topics based on someone’s photos and prompt answers. You still write the opener, with a few ideas to help you get started.

Hinge also has a “Hidden Words” feature that lets you filter unwanted words, phrases, and emoji in comments attached to incoming likes. Verification requirements vary by region, with biometric Face Check required in some locations.

Match is worth a look if you’re over 40, want a relationship, and like having enough profile detail to work out whether someone interests you. It’s my pick for detailed profiles, particularly if you want to explain your hobbies, family life, and relationship goals in more detail.

It also has a history of reaching older daters. In the 2026 SSRS survey, 33 percent of U.S. adults aged 50 and older who had ever used a dating site or app said they’d tried Match. That put it second among the platforms listed for that age group.

If you’re returning to dating after divorce or losing a partner, the profile format gives you space to explain what you’re looking for now. Maybe you want to remarry, find a regular travel companion, or meet someone who understands that your custody schedule determines which weekends you’re free.

I picked Match because its profiles let you picture how someone might fit into your life. Interests, lifestyle details, and relationship preferences provide useful starting points when you’re deciding who you’d like to meet.

Erica Arrechea, founder and CEO of Cinqe Matchmaking, describes the practical questions that can shape later-life dating: “Do we live together? Do we get married? Do we travel together but keep separate homes? How involved are our children? Where do we spend holidays?"

Those are the kinds of considerations I’d keep in mind while browsing. A shared love of travel is a conversation starter; finding out whether your schedules and expectations line up helps you decide where that conversation might go.

You can browse profiles before subscribing, and mutual matches can message each other for free. That makes it easier to get a feel for the people nearby before deciding whether a paid plan is worth your money.

Match’s reporting tools let you flag concerns from a profile or message, including harassment, requests for money, and inappropriate behavior during an in-person date. Reports are anonymous.

Its subscription history also deserves a mention. In August 2025, Match Group agreed to a $14 million FTC settlement over allegations involving misleading subscription guarantees, account restrictions after unsuccessful billing disputes, and difficult cancellation processes. The agreement required clearer disclosures and simpler cancellation mechanisms — relevant context if you’re considering a paid plan.

Read our full review of AdultFriendFinder.

Bumble is worth trying if you’re over 40, looking for a relationship, and ready to see someone other than the same three people in your Hinge feed. Profile prompts and dating intentions give you a starting point, and you can match and chat without paying for a subscription.

If you’ve lost track of who’s allowed to message first, fair. Bumble introduced "Opening Moves," which let men respond to a woman’s prompt, then removed the feature in Australia and Mexico. In August 2026, it made a broader change: Either person can now send the first message. You get one opener, and the conversation stays locked until the recipient replies. They have 72 hours to respond.

That takes some pressure off women who are tired of thinking up every opening line, while keeping the other person in control of whether the chat continues. If you’re juggling work, family commitments, or a calendar booked three weekends out, the longer reply window is welcome breathing room.

I picked Bumble because it has useful tools for fitting dating around the rest of your life. "Snooze Mode" is one of my favorites: You can pause your visibility to new people for a day, a week, or indefinitely while keeping your existing conversations. When you need a break, your profile can wait until you’re ready to pick things up again.

If getting your profile together is the part you’re dreading, Bumble’s AI Profile Guidance and AI Photo Feedback offer suggestions on your bio and photos. Profile Guidance launched globally, while Photo Feedback initially launched in the U.S. A little help may be welcome when you’ve rewritten “a typical Sunday” so many times you’ve forgotten what you do on Sundays.

Bumble also has practical tools for meeting someone new. ID Verification checks your government-issued ID and a live selfie, while "Share Date" lets you send a trusted contact your match’s name and photo, plus when and where you’re meeting. It makes the “here’s who I’m going out with” text easier to put together.

There’s one issue I’m still hung up on. In 2025, users reported seeing people they’d already blocked, prompting founder Whitney Wolfe Herd to publicly promise improvements to trust and safety. That history still factors into my recommendation.

OkCupid is my pick for values-driven matches, especially if you’re over 40 and know which differences you can happily live with — and which ones would turn dinner into a debate you’ve already had too many times. Its matching questions give you a way to compare views on politics, relationships, and everyday habits before starting a conversation.

It’s also worth considering if mainstream profile options have left you feeling boxed in. OkCupid offers over 60 ways to identify across gender and orientation and lets you specify what kind of relationship you want. Whether you’re looking for monogamy, exploring non-monogamy, or dating without a wedding deadline, you can put those intentions on your profile.

I picked OkCupid because its questions give you something specific to consider as you browse. You answer questions about yourself and what you’d accept in a partner, and those responses help shape your match percentages. You can spend time on the subjects you care about, whether that’s religion, political beliefs, or how someone approaches a relationship.

That format works well when you have an established life and want to share it with someone whose priorities match yours. A funny bio might get your attention, but someone’s answers can give you a specific question to ask — or a shared opinion to bond over. Since the free version lets you browse, match, and chat, you can take that curiosity into a conversation without paying for a subscription.

Tinder is my pick for casual dating over 40, whether you’re easing back into the scene after a long relationship or enjoying being single and seeing where things go. You can keep your profile straightforward, browse nearby people, and chat with mutual matches for free.

It’s also a place to be direct about what you want. The "Relationship Goals" feature lets you display the kind of connection you’re looking for, so “something casual” doesn’t have to become an awkward reveal three conversations in. If your plans are flexible, you can say that, too.

I picked Tinder because getting started doesn’t require a lengthy questionnaire. You both swipe right, you match, and either person can message first.

The experience still depends on your local crowd. In this r/datingoverforty discussion, recommendations vary by location, and people describe different levels of success across the same apps. Tinder is worth comparing with your other options, particularly if you keep seeing the same faces elsewhere.

Your bio gives someone a reason to choose you out of that swipe deck. Mention the concert you’re excited for or your strong opinions about the best breakfast spot in town. Give a potential match an easier opening than “So, what brings you here?”

If you’d feel more comfortable bringing friends along, Tinder’s Group Hangouts let you turn meeting new people into a group outing. One person picks an activity (like karaoke) and invites at least two friends. Once your group has three members, you can browse other groups, match, and chat about getting together. Everyone needs their own Tinder profile, and the feature is available in the U.S. and select markets.

Tinder has also expanded "Face Check," its video-selfie verification process. The scan checks that you’re a live person, compares your face with your profile photos, and looks for the same face across multiple accounts. It involves biometric data: Tinder says it deletes the video after review and retains encrypted facial data for verification and duplicate-account detection. That’s worth knowing before you sign up.

eharmony is for the over-40 dater who wants a long-term relationship and has the patience for a thorough sign-up process. When I tested it, the questionnaire asked about everything from why I wanted a relationship to whether I’d prefer sharing a bed or sleeping in separate bedrooms. If you like thinking through those details before browsing, there’s plenty to consider here.

You’ll also need a budget. The free experience left me scrolling through blurred photos and encountering frequent subscription prompts, which made it difficult to get excited about the people I might meet.

I picked eharmony for its detailed approach to compatibility, though it wouldn’t be my first recommendation for everyone. The questionnaire explores relationship expectations, everyday habits, and how you react when someone upsets you. Some questions gave me useful things to think about; others had me wondering how much longer I’d be sitting there choosing between pictures of shapes.

I entered details about my work, education, children, and marital status, then answered prompts and wrote a bio. If you’re dating after divorce or losing a partner, those profile details can help explain your circumstances without having to repeat the basics in every conversation.

What frustrated me was getting through all that and still being unable to see my featured matches’ photos without paying. My first suggested profile was two and a half hours away, and the other two were also over an hour away. That was my experience in a small Virginia town, but it’s a useful reminder to check the recommendations you receive before committing to a subscription.

I also found the upgrade process pushy. A “Welcome Gift” turned out to be a subscription discount, and clicking through took me to a payment screen. I could back out and continue with the free version, but the experience made paying feel like the expected next step.

For someone who wants detailed compatibility information and is comfortable paying to use the service, eharmony may earn a spot on the shortlist. My own experience puts it behind Hinge and Match: I wanted to spend more time getting to know potential dates and less time getting through sign-up and subscription screens.

Hinge is my pick for the best dating app for people over 40, particularly if you want a relationship and prefer getting a sense of someone’s personality before matching. You can like or comment on a specific photo or prompt, giving you a more natural conversation starter than a generic “hey.”

It isn’t the only option worth trying. Match is worth comparing if you want more detailed profiles, while Tinder is an option for casual dating. Start with the free experience, see who’s nearby, and then decide whether to commit to a subscription.

Yes. Hinge is my top recommendation: You can send a limited number of likes, attach comments, and chat with mutual matches without subscribing. Paid plans add benefits, but you don’t need one to have a conversation.

OkCupid, Bumble, and Tinder are other options to compare. When choosing a free dating app, look beyond “free to sign up” and check whether you can match and message without paying.

There’s no universal answer. Your experience depends on where you live, who you want to meet, and how dating fits around your existing commitments. Being over 40 doesn’t automatically mean you’re more confident, looking for marriage, or interested only in people with the same relationship history. Instead of choosing an app based on age alone, think about the life you want to share.

I’d start with Tinder if you’re exploring casual dating and Bumble if you want an alternative with more structure around opening conversations. Neither is automatically better because you’re over 40, and I wouldn’t choose Bumble solely for its old “women message first” reputation.

Try the free versions and compare the people you see within your preferred age range and distance. Daters in the r/datingoverforty community report different experiences depending on their location, so someone else’s favorite may not be your best local option.

Use recent photos, say what kind of connection you want, and give someone a glimpse of what spending time with you would look like. Specific details — your Sunday hiking routine, love of terrible horror movies, or search for a regular doubles partner — give people more to respond to than “I enjoy having fun.”

You don’t need to write a résumé or disclose your relationship history. Mention the priorities that affect compatibility, like having children or wanting a relationship without living together.

“Make sure to select recent photos as it can be misleading to use photos of you when you were younger,” Weiss tells Mashable.

Protect your personal information, meet somewhere public, and let a trusted friend know your plans. A video call can help you get a better sense of someone before meeting.

“Meet in a public place, as usual, and have a friend check in with you later in the night or the next morning to make sure you’re OK,” Weiss advises.

Never send money or gifts to an online love interest you haven’t met in person. If you suspect a scam, stop communicating, report the account, and talk to someone you trust.

Pay attention to patterns of pressure, inconsistency, and financial requests — not just an awkward bio or a bad profile photo.

Requests for money for travel, medical bills, or another supposed emergency.

Offers to teach you how to invest, particularly in cryptocurrency.

Repeated excuses for why they can’t meet.

Profile photos that appear under another name in a reverse-image search.

Pressure to move off the app immediately or disregard your boundaries is also a reason to slow down. “Steer away from anything that requests payment or asks you to move to another platform right away,” Weiss says.

I wouldn’t make an exclusive app your first stop simply because you’re an established professional. An application process or selective membership doesn’t tell you whether someone shares your goals — or whether there will be enough people nearby you want to meet.

For this guide, I’m prioritizing apps I can recommend on their everyday usefulness: profiles, messaging access, preferences, and the experience of finding potential dates. I’d try those before treating exclusivity as a reason to sign up.

Choosing a dating app shouldn’t require downloading six of them and paying for three subscriptions. I’ve spent years testing dating apps for Mashable, and this guide draws on that hands-on experience, expert commentary, and feedback from daters over 40. Here’s what goes into my recommendations:

Hands-on testing: I create profiles, browse potential matches, and use the messaging tools to see how each app works. I try the free experience and evaluate paid upgrades, paying particular attention to what you can do without subscribing. Free registration doesn’t mean much if you can’t see profiles or have a conversation.

Relevance to dating over 40: I look at how well each app lets you communicate your relationship goals, interests, and everyday priorities, including children, lifestyle preferences, and plans for the future. I also consider whether useful filters are available for free or locked behind a subscription. An app doesn’t earn a place here just because it markets itself to “mature singles.”

Expert and community perspectives: I consult relationship professionals who aren’t affiliated with dating apps and read Reddit discussions and app-store reviews for perspectives beyond my own. Feedback from people dating in their 40s and beyond helps identify recurring frustrations, but I don’t treat an individual success story (or a terrible date) as proof of what everyone will experience.

Ongoing reassessment: I revisit recommendations as features, messaging rules, subscription benefits, and ownership change. If an app changes substantially, its previous review isn’t enough to justify keeping it on the list.

#513. The best Kindle and e-reader accessories for your coziest reading nook yet

Kindles are the darling device of BookTok, where you can scroll through thousands of videos on the best accessories and gadgets to maximize your reading experience. One thing about the BookTok girlies: They're right. While I've spent hours watching videos of people decking out their Kindles with accessories, I never really understood the extras until I tried them for myself.

Kindle accessories are add-ons like remote page turners, gooseneck stands, clear cases, PopSockets, and hand straps, which are all aimed at improving your reading comfort. These accessories are so popular that even Amazon launched two of its own new accessories in 2026.

You may roll your eyes at a gooseneck stand or page-turning remote — I once did — but you're missing out on a life of luxury. A life that includes a Kindle on a stand, a remote page turner in hand, and you all tucked into the covers.

And keep in mind that while Kindles are the buzziest e-readers, there's a whole lot of love for Kobo e-readers on BookTok and here at Mashable. Even though the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is our favorite e-reader, we still have a lot of love for the Kobo Clara Colour and Kobo Libra Colour.

So if you own a Kindle or use another e-reader, this guide is for you: It features the essential accessories, including stands, remotes, grips, and cases. Plus, all the recently launched remotes from Kobo and Boox.

Remote page turners rose in popularity on BookTok, so much so that Amazon finally launched its own, the Kindle Click, which is compatible with 2024 Kindles or newer.

At the end of the night, when you want to be cozy in bed, tucked under the blanket to stay warm, the remote allows you to do just that. Combined with the gooseneck stand? Nighttime reading is about to be the coziest it's ever been.

And while the page turner is great for getting cozy, it's also ideal for when you're using a Kindle while on the treadmill.

Amazon now makes the Kindle Click, joining the likes of Kobo, Boox, and Durobo. While the Boox Tappy and Durobo Moodi aren't my favorite, the Kobo remote is perfectly designed.

While we expected a Kindle remote to join Amazon's latest batch of Kindles, the more surprising accessory is the new Page Turn Cover. It works seamlessly with Kindles, attaching via magnetic Pogo pins. Once connected, you can use the buttons on the case to turn the page.

It works like a charm, but there's a big catch. The Page Turn Cover only works with the Paperwhite Signature Edition and Colorsoft Signature Edition e-readers, meaning to use the case, you need to have one of those e-readers. Not to mention, the case costs $79.99.

That being said, I love the Page Turn Cover and think it's a worthy investment.

While the remote page turner helps you click through your book, to go truly hands-free, you need to prop up your e-reader, too. Enter the gooseneck stand. After seeing this viral video, I, and the rest of the internet, was influenced to get a clip-in stand for an e-reader.

And let me tell you, it is a luxury to have this stand. While a Kindle is still lightweight, when you're on a reading marathon, your arm inevitably gets tired from holding up the device. But having a gooseneck stand positions the Kindle within reading distance without any arm fatigue.

To test out a gooseneck stand, I tried the Magipea Gooseneck Stand, which is compatible with either a Kindle or Kobo e-reader (I use it with both). I find the bendy arm of this stand to be a little too stiff, but overall, it still works well.

There are plenty of Kindle cases in the sea, but the most popular option among BookTok is a simple, clear case. Sure, that seems boring, but the exciting part is decorating it. Add-ons like charms also bring personal flair, and some people even buy inserts or stickers to swap out over time.

And if you're interested in using a PopSockets grip with your Kindle, I recommend getting a case that's MagSafe compliant so you can take it on and off. PopSockets has its own Kindle case that also happens to be MagSafe.

PopSockets are already the best ergonomic grip for your phone, so why wouldn't they be the best grip for another handheld device? When I'm not using my Kindle with the gooseneck stand, I like using it with a PopSockets grip for an ergonomic hold.

With a traditional PopSockets grip, you attach it to a device with adhesive, but that means once it's on, it's on. But using a MagSafe PopSockets grip allows you to attach and reattach the grip, depending on whether you want your Kindle to lie flat.

I personally use the PopSockets MagSafe Kick-Out Stand with my Kindle since that's what I use on my phone, and I like that I can prop it up to stand vertically. However, PopSockets launched a line of bookish MagSafe grips to go with its line of Kindle cases.

If PopSockets grips aren't really your thing, then Strapsicle makes a nice alternative. Strapsicle's straps attach to the corners of your e-reader, creating a cross pattern. Your hand then slips through the straps, delivering an easy hold on your e-reader. While I personally prefer the feel of a PopSockets grip, the Strapsicle lets your hand lie flat, so it doesn't cramp up from being in a hold. The Strapsicle works best when it has a snug fit, so using it with a case can be a little tight.

#512. Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year

Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.

From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment.

Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds.

All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell.

"If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds Director of Insights Ivan Drury.

Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive.

And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive.

These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down.

There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place.

"I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data."

The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.

The Toyota RAV4, which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand.

The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck.

The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani.

"We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said.

Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.

Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback.

"You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.

The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla.

The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990 and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000.

"Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."

Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars have risen and are up more than almost any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used-car market.

Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars.

Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly 3 in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost.

Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.

Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said.

The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said.

"It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."

Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said.

"The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to. Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."

The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer.

"The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

#510. NASA’s Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth. Here’s What to Know About the Impending Impact

After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft—which is roughly as big as a large elevator—will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low.

What is now a useless piece of space junk was for a long time extraordinarily valuable to the scientific community. Launched on November 20, 2004, Swift was a space observatory equipped with three telescopes. It was designed primarily to detect and study gamma-ray bursts, which are among the most energetic explosions in the universe. Swift would locate these events and transmit their positions to observatories around the world for further study.

The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about the evolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and the destruction of stars by black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without a propulsion system capable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered.

In July 2026, NASA launched a special $30 million mission to rescue Swift. A robotic spacecraft called LINK was supposed to drag Swift away from Earth by 150 miles, giving it a higher orbit and thus extending its operational life. Unfortunately, LINK failed. In August, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the difficulties that led to the mission’s cancellation were due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system, which made it impossible to keep it properly oriented and stable in space.

On October 26, NASA announced that Swift was less than 170 miles from Earth’s surface—a very low orbit for a satellite. According to the agency, the telescopes on board could no longer maintain stable observations of their astronomical targets. Swift conducted its final observation on October 20, then the operations team based at Pennsylvania State University terminated its operational status.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters in Washington, said in a statement. “In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community.”

In its lifetime, the satellite observed over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and nearly as many supernovas, data from which contributed to more than 7,000 research papers. And its contributions are far from over. “Swift leaves us with an extraordinary archive of multiwavelength observations that will fuel new discoveries for decades more,” Domagal-Goldman added.

The Swift satellite is shown in July 2004 at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

The US Space Force estimates Swift is likely to crash on or around Friday, November 6—or at least whatever remains of the satellite will. Most of the space observatory is expected to disintegrate as it reenters the atmosphere. However, some pieces made of tungsten and parts of the mirrors could survive that chaotic process, Brad Cenko, NASA’s chief scientist for the mission, told the Associated Press.

“The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors,” Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components, said to Space.com. “Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down—nothing recognizable as a telescope.”

Where exactly will that debris fall? Large areas of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America fall within the reentry zone monitored by the Space Force. If there is a more precise calculation, that information has not been made public, but it’s most likely that all Swift’s remaining pieces will end up in the ocean.

“NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published,” Sladen said regarding the risk assessment. “Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork.”

#509. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."
