#508. The 8 best headphones of 2026: We tested the top contenders from Sony, Apple, Bose, and Beats

In 2026, a pair of headphones or earbuds is pretty much non-optional. That's why there are hundreds of different headphones shapes, sizes, styles, colors, and, of course, prices. These days, you can grab a random pair off the digital shelf without too much research and find that they do the job just fine. However, if you're tired of settling for "just fine," then it's worth investing in the best headphones available.

But be warned: The latest generation of flagship noise-cancelling headphones from the likes of Apple, Sony, and Bose will set you back $450 or more, though we have options to recommend for every price range.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

To help you find the best pair of headphones possible, our experts test headphones year-round, from popular models to new releases to budget picks (you can learn more about our detailed testing standards below). The result of that vetting is this guide, which we keep updated regularly to give you the most accurate and current purchasing information possible. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Read our full review of the Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones.

Audiophiles and custom equalizer fans: After three years, Sony's flagship wireless headphones finally got an update. If you love Sony headphones and have an old pair of XM4s, then we can definitely recommend an upgrade. However, if you just purchased a pair of XM5s, then it might be harder to justify an instant upgrade. That said, the active noise cancellation is better than ever, and there are noticeable improvements to audio quality (even if they lose out by a smidge to the latest Technics AZ100 earbuds). Besides music lovers, travelers will also appreciate the new Sony cans, as they fold up and come with an improved travel case.

Mashable's Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth reviewed the XM6 headphones ahead of their launch, and he was impressed with the overall quality. As Werth wrote in his review, "The new Sony headphones offer impressive audio quality, and they definitely improve on the XM5 models. The active noise cancellation is particularly phenomenal...I really appreciated the overall balance, depth, and quality of the audio. For the XM6, Sony audio engineers worked with music mastering engineers here in the United States, and the results are clear when you listen to music. Like all headphone reviewers, I have a dedicated playlist for testing new audio products, and I found that vocal-heavy tracks sound particularly great, with noticeable improvements over the XM5s."

Sony introduced (or, rather, brought back) a major design change for the XM6 headphones — they fold up for easier storage. They're definitely more compact and easier to travel with compared to the previous-gen model. The overall design looks similar, so if you're a fan of the Sony aesthetic, you'll still appreciate how they look.

We do wish there had been slightly bigger improvements after a three-year wait, and the battery life (30 hours with ANC engaged) is the same as the XM5 model, which we also loved. These headphones did arrive with a higher sticker price, so if you can't quite swing the $448 price tag, look for the excellent XM5 headphones on sale.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones (2nd gen).

Those who want the best of the best: For anyone who's yet to buy into the Bose QuietComfort Ultra line, but wants noise-cancelling headphones that can easily handle long hours of wear, there's no better choice than the second generation Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones.

The best noise-cancelling headphones aren't much use if they squeeze your head too tight or prevent you from wearing accessories like earrings or glasses comfortably. In other words, comfort is key — we were big fans of Bose's first gen QC Ultra headphones for exactly this reason.

With the second generation of the headphones, Bose makes minor improvements to the soundscape, noise-cancelling, and somehow the wear. They also fixed other bugs that detracted from the otherwise premium experience of using the QC Ultras.

As a first step, Bose upped the battery life from 24 to 30 hours per charge with ANC. They also added options for wired playback with the USB-C cable (which can simultaneously charge the headphones) or the auxiliary cable for passive playback (which wasn't available on the first gen headphones). In tandem with the battery life, these headphones become much stronger contenders for travel.

For day-to-day use, Bose's noise cancelling remains as solid as ever (though Sony's XM6s are ever so slightly more adept at handling high pitched frequencies), while offering an easy adjustment on 10 different levels of ANC via the companion app. As for the listening experience, the immersive audio remains as lackluster as it did on the first gen, but the overall sound profile came through richer and more robust when we compared the headphones side by side. Bose also added quality of life adjustments like better wear detection, and a lay flat mode that puts the headphones into a low power mode when they're placed face down. Overall, it's hard to beat this blend of sound quality, ANC, and comfort, making the second iteration of the QC Ultras one of our top picks for headphones.

Value fiends: If you don't particularly care to have the most premium pair of headphones on the market (or care to spend several hundred dollars on them), the JLab JBuds Lux ANC headphones are the best budget headphones available. They have functional ANC, decent comfort, great sound balance, and a killer battery life, all with a design that doesn't feel cheap.

At their regular sale price of around $50, these are about a ninth the price of the latest Sony headphones, and a seventh of the price of the Bose QuietComfort headphones, which feel like these headphones' premium analogue.

With budget headphones, it's good to understand what you're trading off from the jump. In the case of these JLab headphones, the ANC will dampen a good amount of environmental sound, from talking coworkers to loud fans, but it won't completely silence the world around you. The app can lag some (we had to exit out of it a few times during testing when it froze), and the fit of these headphones might not be for everyone. For one of our testers, these headphones squeezed their head more than usual (though some users on Reddit called these the most comfortable headphones they've tried). Regardless of the fit, you're likely to hear some creaking from time to time when you move your head around.

At $80, these are all cons that may not be ideal, but are fair for the price point. At these headphones' frequent sale prices that hover in the $50 to $55 range, these cons are even easier to swallow, especially when you consider how these headphones actually sound.

To be clear, you'll likely need to play around with the EQ some to find your perfect settings — we found the first preset to be on the bass-heavy end. Once you do, it's impressive the way these headphones can balance a song. Every part of Panic! At The Disco's "Northern Downpour" shone through, from the vocals, lead guitar, bass, and piano. For budget headphones, we might expect some muddying through these elements, but the JLab JBuds held up great. If we're being nitpicky, The Beatles' "In My Life" came through somewhat dimmer sounding than expected, but not necessarily muddy.

Beyond the sound signature, these headphones have a reasonable amount of customization with the app, especially for their price point. You can adjust the button commands on one of the three on-ear buttons, adjust the ANC intensity with a slider in the app, and create your own custom EQ settings. Multipoint pairing is available, as are spatial audio, music, and movie modes.

Check out our full guide to the best Sony headphones.

Students, casual users, and anyone looking for great sound on the cheap: The new price of entry for flagship noise-cancelling headphones? A cool $450, at least. So, if you're looking for wireless headphones with true active noise cancellation but don't want to spend more than $100, then go with Sony's mid-range noise-cancellers. They have Sony's signature sound (and signature all-plastic design, sadly), and you can almost always find them on sale for under $100 at Amazon and other retailers.

These headphones perform much better than you'd expect a pair of $100 cans to perform. They have surprisingly impressive ANC and multipoint pairing, as well as impressive sound — hardly a surprise with a pair of Sony headphones.

As our reviewer Alex Bracetti wrote, "The WH-CH720 employs 30mm drivers and exclusive brand technologies to broaden sound performance. Expect a vibrant mix of impactful bass with striking mids and highs. Turning on DSEE raises fidelity on poor-quality recordings, which many luxury headphones can’t do. You can tweak the sound to your liking via the EQ, though the headphones sound great on their default setting."

Read our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

Folks too busy to charge their devices: If you're just a little too familiar with the low battery sound on your headphones, the absurdly long battery life on the Nothing Headphone (a) gets you as close as you can to a guarantee that you'll hear it as little as possible. Plus, it has a standout retro design.

Picking the headphones with the best battery life isn't a terribly complex process. That said, it isn't just about picking the pair that can pack the most hours — it's about finding the headphones with the best combination of value, overall performance, and, of course, battery life.

Our standard before was set at 60 hours, which is a great deal higher than the 30 hours you'll find on the Bose and Sony headphones on this list. The Nothing Headphone (a) absolutely blows that standard out of the water, offering 75 hours per charge with ANC on, and 135 hours without.

They check the remaining boxes at $199, which, while not dirt cheap, is a fair deal cheaper than most $400+ flagship models. The sound quality is clear and robust, the noise cancellation will get the job done (if not flawlessly), and the on-ear controls are truly a thing of perfection. During testing, we almost never reached for our devices when adjusting settings because the on-ear controls made it so easy not to. Rounding out the experience is a companion app that's easy to navigate, with features like an eight-band equalizer designed to make your music sound just to your liking.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd gen).

Travelers, students, and anyone blending comfort and value: A lot about our most comfortable headphones pick sounds great, but you're caught up on the price point — understandable. Though a truly excellent, well-rounded headphones experience often comes with a higher price point, Bose's latest headphones — the second generation QuietComforts — prove that investment doesn't need to exceed $400 (for now).

If you're looking for extreme comfort, quality ANC, warm and balanced sound, and a few extras without totally breaking the bank, these are your headphones.

These aren't perfect headphones. The sound profile isn't the most customizable with a three-band equalizer, there's no truly passive playback with the wired connections, the noise cancellation will get staticky during a plane takeoff, and the battery life leans on the low side at 24 hours (finding 30 hours or up isn't too hard these days on a pair of over-ear headphones).

All this to say, these aren't technically perfect headphones, but those cons pale in comparison to their pros. At $359, these headphones are nearly $100 cheaper than the Bose QC Ultra 2 headphones, but offer many of the same features. For starters, the comfort and noise cancellation are nearly on par with the significantly more expensive headphones, which is to say it's very, very good — like easily wearable for a full day of travel. The tactile controls are intuitive and functional, the colorways are varied and unique while remaining appealing, and there's an Immersive Audio listening mode for changing up how you hear your music.

In a time when most tech prices are rising, it's refreshing to see a brand release a pair of headphones that strive for ultra-premium performance, while sticking to a more mildly premium price point.

Read our original review of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones, or see how they compare to the new XM6 headphones.

Last-gen lovers: If you want a premium pair of Sony noise-cancelling headphones but refuse to pay more than $400 for a pair of headphones, we feel you. We also have good news: The XM5 headphones hold up well in 2026, and they're still worth the investment, especially when they're on sale.

Originally released in 2022, the Sony XM5 headphones are still legendary. They had unbeatable ANC and sound for the money, and even in 2026, they sound shockingly good. That's because the new flagship XM6 model only made iterative improvements over these cans. So, now that they go on sale for as little as $248, you just can't write off the older XM5s.

This Mashable Choice product received a 4.7 out of 5 stars in our original review, and even when we recently compared them head-to-head with their successors, they performed incredibly well.

We won't beat around the bush: There's no definitive "best" product here. Sure, elite audio brands put out high-quality products across the board, but even within each of those brands, you'll find different tiers of products. Some will deliver better value, and some will deliver better hardware and active noise cancellation.

All this to say, the best pair of earbuds or headphones largely comes down to personal preference and how you plan to use them. Some listeners swear by over-ear headphones, while others prefer the minimalism of earbuds — one is not necessarily better than the other. Athletes who like to use headphones at the gym will appreciate waterproof materials and the best open earbuds, while frequent fliers will prefer devices with long battery life, comfort, and portability. Finally, music lovers and audiophiles will want to invest in premium features like a custom equalizer, spatial audio, or best-in-class active noise cancellation.

To help you pick your pair, we tested all of the headphones in this guide (and a lot that didn't make the cut). Here, you'll find the top headphones of 2026 for noise cancellation, music, price, and wired connections.

We focused primarily on the best wireless headphones for this guide. While wired headphones have their fans, wireless headphones are just more convenient for most of us, though some of us are also fans of Apple's EarPods. With the release of the new noise-cancelling wired earbuds from Bose, we will be keeping our testing pool open to more wired models and will update this guide accordingly, should any earn a spot.

Most recently, we tested the Marshall Monitor III, JBL Tour One M3 headphones, and the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC, and though they had their merits, they fell short of winning the best of the best spot on this guide.

We've also tested the Sonos Ace headphones and Dyson OnTrac headphones. And while we loved them both for sound quality and noise cancellation, they fare in the way of AirPods Max — left out of our recommendations for their high price points.

August 2026: Following the release of the second generation Bose QuietComfort headphones, we've added them to our list as the best budget pick from Bose for headphones.

March 2025: We've designated the Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 earbuds as the most comfortable ANC earbuds and crowned the Sony XM6 earbuds as the new best noise-cancelling earbuds.

December 2025: We replaced the Jabra Elite 8 Active Gen 2 earbuds, which are no longer available, with the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 sports earbuds.

December 2025: We removed the Marshall Mode wired earbuds, as they're frequently out of stock.

December 2025: We added the Sony WH-CH720N Noise-Canceling Headphones as the best headphones under $100.

December 2025: We added the Sony XM5 headphones, originally released in 2022, as our new honorable mention pick.

August 2026: We replaced the Sennheiser Momentum 4 with the Nothing Headphone (a) as our best battery life pick.

A few major headphone releases happened in September: Sony's mid-range WH-10000XM4C headphones, Sony's budget WH-CH730N headphones, and the Beats 360, the first pair of over-ear headphones from the brand in three years. From Bose, we've also recently seen new wired noise-cancelling earbuds, as well as two new pairs of open earbuds. We'll be comparing them against our current picks to see if they have a spot among our favorites.

No, we didn't forget to include the iconic Apple AirPods Max in our guide to the best headphones. It's not that we don't like them — in fact, we think they sound and look great (emphasis on look). However, after testing and re-testing them, we think they're just too expensive to justify a wholehearted recommendation. While we appreciate that they now (finally) come with lossless audio, they're still behind on features like battery life.

While they're still a smart choice for style-conscious Apple fans, we can no longer include them among the elite. We thought they were way too expensive upon their initial release, and we only feel more firm in this position six years later.

While the long-anticipated AirPods Max 2 are finally out, our reviewer found the upgrades to be minimal. At the same $549 the original Maxes were released at, these headphones are just too expensive and underperforming for us to recommend them.

Like with most products, this comes down to personal preference, but there are a few brands known for making really solid headphones. For those who appreciate quality ANC above all else, Bose headphones will be the best brand. Enjoy a rich and balanced sound profile? You'll want to check out Sony. In the budget space, Anker Soundcore products have impressed us lately. Still, we recommend reading each of our above picks to see which speaks most to you.

If you're wondering what headphones you've been seeing all over your For You page, it's likely a pair of Sonys, either the older WH-1000XM5s or the brand new Sony WH-1000XM6s. The former two used to be our top picks, but the XM6s now take the crown. Beats headphones are also incredibly popular, especially as brands like Marshall and Jabra fall out of favor.

Other than those, the Bose QuietComfort line is a popular pick, especially for those who wear their headphones for long periods of time. And of course, Apple AirPods are a popular pick for iPhone users who prefer earbuds over headphones. We're not huge fans of the AirPods Max, though, as we think they're too overpriced for what they offer. However, with Apple's recent updates to the AirPods line, we know they are top of mind.

Every single pair of headphones we included in this guide was hands-on tested by a Mashable reporter, editor, or contributor. You can learn about our in-depth process by taking a look at the standardized testing guide we developed for this category.

Below, you'll find our condensed testing criteria for headphones:

We listened to a wide variety of genres of music, podcasts, and other forms of media. If a pair didn't at least sound solid across the board, they didn't make our list. In this category, we also considered the quality (and existence) of any equalizers.

We'll test ANC power around our homes as we work, with and without an audio assist, and outdoors. If headphones have customizable ANC levels, or automatic switching between noise-cancelling modes, we make sure that they actually provide noticeable differences in performance.

Everything from comfort to touch controls fall under this category. We look at what headphones offer to provide the best wear for the greatest amount of people, whether that be a strong selection of earbud tip sizes or particularly soft padding. Whenever possible, we test and re-test headphones over longer periods of time to see how they hold up.

We evaluate how headphones perform in all of the above categories, and if that performance matches their price point.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for three years at Mashable.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

#506. ‘Our Risk, Their Reward’: Zohran Mamdani on AI and Data Centers

If you think you had a wild year, just imagine how New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani must feel.

In October 2025, weeks before his historic election win, WIRED sat down with Mamdani for an interview at his campaign office. I remember, vividly, the energy that he carried into the room. This was a man, after all, who’d just pulled off a stunning political feat, rising from being an unknown to becoming the mayoral front-runner in a matter of months. In part, that was because of his message, which focused squarely on affordability and the working class. But much of Mamdani’s campaign success can be attributed to how that message was delivered, namely through a mastery of social media that made every other politician in America look like they were still figuring out how to open Instagram.

Mamdani, then just about to turn 34, radiated in our first conversation with what I can best describe as a supernatural electricity. It lit up the room, and in a subsequent photo shoot on a bustling Manhattan street, drew passersby as if by magic. New Yorkers hooted and hollered at the candidate who, seemingly overnight, had made the mundanity of local politics feel like a cultural revolution.

Fast-forward one year, and the Mamdani electricity is still there—it just might be a little bit more tired. The daily grind of governing, after all, doesn’t offer quite the same excitement as a rocket-ship campaign. Not to mention that Mamdani, particularly given his massive reach online, has now become a lightning rod for polarizing conversations, from Israel to the Democratic Socialists of America, as well as a beacon of political hope for millions across the country and even around the world.

Mamdani’s approval rating among Big Apple voters sits at a stunning 69 percent, and he’s become among the most influential figures on the American left; he’s also been described, by his harshest critics, as a dangerous radical whose politics threaten the very city he’s been elected to lead. No pressure.

During a sit-down interview at New York’s City Hall, the mayor and I spoke about what he’s learned during his 10 months on the job, how he uses social media as a tool for governance, and where he stands on some of the most pressing issues facing Americans in today’s midterm elections. Mamdani might be tired—he divulged, hoarsely, that it had been “a long day”—but the internet’s Mayor also seems newly liberated, and certainly empowered to speak his mind. Winning power and wielding it, after all, are two very different things. And right now, the power is squarely in Zohran Mamdani’s corner.

KATIE DRUMMOND: It was almost exactly this time last year that I interviewed you in your campaign office. I remember that for two reasons. One, it was just before the election, but two, you were just about to have a birthday. I was remembering that this weekend, because I was in Sunset Park on Saturday. Sunset Park, for those who don't know, is the best park in Brooklyn, and actually all of New York. I'm sure you agree.

While I was there, I saw you being serenaded with “Happy Birthday.” I did not join. I kept walking. I was like, “I’m gonna see this guy.”

ZOHRAN MAMDANI: I was wondering, like, “Who’s that woman who’s not singing along?”

Yes, the one with the really excited 9-year-old, and her mom was like, “No, we’re gonna keep going.” That was me.

Do you feel a year older? How has the last year of your life been?

It’s been a pretty incredible year. It has also been probably the most transformative year that I’ve lived in my life in terms of what my life was versus what it is now. Much of that year has been having the privilege of having the greatest job in the world. To lead this city and now to be 35.

I think 35. It’s a funny thing because in the world of my friends, this is an age that has a lot of existential questions that come with it. In the work that I do, most people are significantly older than me, and so the meaning of the age, it doesn’t really live in a professional setting.

Do you ever feel like your age is a barrier in politics?

No. When I met [Brazilian President Luiz Inácio] Lula [da Silva] during the UN General Assembly, he was very excited by the fact that I was young. [Laughs] He kept coming back, “So young!” I don’t think it’s a barrier. It’s been one that has also illuminated both the promises and the betrayals of politics.

To be 35 means you grew up through the housing crisis. You grew up through the Iraq War. You grew up through so much of what has shaped our country’s politics over the last few decades. These have been formative moments in my and so many other people’s lives. That too often politics is shaped by those for whom these are issues that just affect other people, not ones that have been all-consuming.

We spent quite a bit of time last year talking about social media and your campaign’s use of it. WIRED declared you the internet’s Mayor. That was before you even won the election. It was a gamble. We felt pretty good about your odds …

No, absolutely not, and never. You told us that you wanted your campaign to not just do social media better than other candidates; you wanted to “own the medium.” You’re still at it. How are you thinking about social media as a tool now for governance versus a tool for campaigning?

I think the similarity is that you have to continue to recognize the fact that for many New Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums. I say that because if your goal is to reach as many New Yorkers as possible to tell them about a policy that you are unveiling that they could stand to benefit from, your responsibility is then to communicate through every conceivable measure.

Social media means that we can make a video that could reach, that will reach, more than a million people. That’s just on one specific medium. Also, it means that you have to continue to work your way backwards from How are New Yorkers consuming media? It’s not that we have the right answer, it’s just that we’re listening.

For example, we heard from a number of Spanish-speaking New Yorkers that if you really want to communicate with a specific constituency that you’re not reaching right now, you need to make a WhatsApp channel.

So we made a WhatsApp channel, El Chisme Oficial de NYC, and on that channel we will share directly with Spanish-speaking New Yorkers information that we’re putting out, and you will hear voice notes of me speaking in incredibly halting Spanish about what that policy is.

I think for too long there’s been a sense of “pat myself on the back” in government where it’s like, “I put out the paper press release. People should just know. I put this in one obscure place that people could find if they were looking for it.” We have to make politics and political decisions something that reach people wherever they already are, as opposed to the condescension that comes with, “If you’re not reading this, then it’s not meant for you.”

You also talked last year about your time campaigning and feeling like you needed to put yourself out there on social media in different ways, “Many of which are embarrassing.” What does it look like to be less embarrassing on social media now that you’re the mayor?

Have you tried to clean up your act a little bit?

I feel like I’m equally embarrassing. I think there’s a part of social media which is all about the presentation of cool and mystery.

I live in a world where you will know everything about me, and I have to utilize that to try and share the message of what we’re doing and why we’re doing it. I think in some ways that means abandoning any fear of embarrassment or what it means for perception. If the way that you can learn about the Rent Guidelines Board is me jumping into freezing cold water, then so be it.

That’s what it was when I was running for office, and I think today we’re still taking the same approach of: How can we communicate with as many people as possible? How can we not veer into a place of complacency? That “Oh, now that I’m the mayor, it means everything has to conform to a traditional outreach.”

Part of the reason why so many people feel so ambivalent, at best, about politics is that there’s a sense of irrelevance. And some of that irrelevance comes from the focus of politics, but some of it also comes from the methods of politics. If politics continues to present itself in a way that it did 20 years ago, that is ignoring the fact that we are living in a very different world today. That’s the world that we should be speaking to, and that’s the world whose concerns we should be reflecting.

I would just say that in the year since we sat down together, there’s been a lot of focus on our use of the medium, as if that is more important than the message. I think it’s important to focus on the use of medium, the respect for the medium, and also to understand that putting tired, old ideas into a short-form version in a vertical video does not answer the critical issue with politics today.

It’s not just the presentation, it’s also the substance.

The New York Times published a story in September about your office’s work with creators. Your administration works with lots of creators, some of whom receive talking points around initiatives. They’re invited to cover events, sometimes where traditional journalists, people like myself, would not be present. Among the concerns raised in that piece is the idea of this distinction between journalist and creator.

I understand wanting to leverage social media to reach people in new ways. I think that’s really laudable. But how do you think about that distinction between, quote unquote, “professional journalism” and content creation? Because I think for the average person, and people are very smart, that line has become incredibly blurry.

Talking points are essentially the basis of a press release, right? When we announce a new policy, in the press release there’ll be quotes from myself and other relevant agency heads and other relevant politicians, and then there’ll also be a description as to what the policy is.

To me, that is so critical because we’re looking to demystify politics, and some policies are pretty self-explanatory, and other policies are ones that, frankly, if I didn’t have talking points, then I wouldn’t even be able to formulate what that is.

Earlier this week, we announced that we were going to deliver on an innovative solution to flooding in Central Park. We were going to be able to lower the water levels in three key water bodies to ensure that we would do so in advance of a storm, and then prevent the typical storm water runoff. You need to be able to explain that before you have a conversation about it. So that’s where I would push a little bit on the idea of what talking points are and what they serve.

To your question, you have to be able to treat all of these different mediums with respect and understand the differences between them. If we were an administration that exclusively engaged with digital-first creators, then that would be an issue. But what I see as important is we have to speak to journalists for whom their medium is television, newspaper, radio, digital, magazine, as well as those for whom their only medium might be TikTok or Instagram or Twitter or Bluesky, whatever it may be.

It cannot be a choice any longer, because I think, as you’ve said, for many New Yorkers, there is a sense that all of this is media.

I think we have to have respect for that, as opposed to what has long been a political condescension about which media is legitimate and which media is illegitimate.

How do you separate audiences in your mind when you think about what you would say on TikTok or Instagram, what you would say to a journalist, what you would say behind a podium? Do you think about those distinctions?

Not so much. I think if you try to calibrate yourself for every single constituency, you are losing sight of why people will want to listen. It starts to veer into an imitation as opposed to a presentation of the facts, and I think there’s a difference in that we’ll sit down for 48 minutes. But if I put out a video on Instagram that’s 48 minutes, is it gonna do well? No. But if I’m thinking that I should speak like this over there, and then I should speak like this over here, you’re gonna end up kind of twisting and turning yourself into knots.

I want to move to the midterms, but last year we spent some well-earned time talking about Eric Adams’ social media campaign. He did incredible things on those platforms. Remarkable.

Michael Bay. His life has been changed by that one video.

Phenomenal. Who is the Eric Adams of the midterms on social?

The social media that I am still confused by …

… is that of the departing Congressman Shri Thanedar.

I just never fully understand what I’m looking at.

What are you looking at? What’s happening in the videos?

Are we in carousel mode? Is it just a single photo?

Typically solo style. I would invite others to take a look, and I would say that I’m very excited as well about the incoming congressman.

I will take a look. [Laughs] There is some remarkable AI-generated social media content from some candidates, some of which includes AI-generated versions of you talking about, I think it was a delusion pill.

You and Governor Hochul, you’re talking about taking the delusion pill …

… where you think that having higher taxes and less money is a good thing. You should check this out.

Was this from [Republican gubernatorial candidate] Bruce Blakeman?

You are not on the ballot for the midterms this November, but this is a big one. In the last year, you have become one of the most influential people in politics. Whether you agree with me saying that or not, you’ve been described repeatedly as something of a power broker within the Democratic Party. An endorsement from you matters.

I’m curious about your decision to endorse and campaign for Governor Hochul. She's seeking reelection. You were critical of her before taking office. Can you talk us through that calculus and what changed?

I think the key thing that my endorsement is a reflection of is just how productive our working relationship has been. And frankly, it is a stark contrast to that of the typical working relationship between the mayor of New York City and the governor of New York state. You look through the years, frankly, and you will find mayor and governor after mayor and governor who are seemingly forever at loggerheads.

What I've found in working with Governor Hochul is that we can deliver on material wins for working-class New Yorkers. And to me, the single most exciting one of those is Universal 2K. On the eighth day of our administration, she agreed to deliver $1.2 billion to make universal childcare a reality for 2-year-olds in this city.

The two of us spent a morning, maybe about a week or two ago, with a family whose child was enrolled in 2K, and they told us that before that, they had to send their child to a different state, that his grandmother had to drive him at 4:00 am for him to get to a childcare that they could afford, and they were still paying $2,300 a month.

That partnership delivered this family more than $20,000 of savings that they can now put towards a house. That, to me, is what politics has to be. It has to mean something for working people. You don’t have to translate to them what $2,300 a month means. They feel it, they know it.

That’s what I'm excited to build on. To me, it’s her track record. It’s her commitment to this city, one that continued in the budget that we had where we were facing a significant fiscal deficit, and she was a real partner in ensuring that we could deliver a balanced budget. There’s a stark contrast with her opponent, who is a little more busy with AI-generated videos of the two of us.

He’s been very busy making AI-generated videos, and defending ICE. I could go on.

Yes, which is a combination that I think most New Yorkers would not want to see in the governor’s office. I also think that his response to universal childcare was to say this was a delivery of a benefit to lazy parents. I have yet to meet a lazy parent in New York City.

I meet people who are exhausted by the fact that our city and our country has made parenthood something that is incredibly difficult to do and seen as if it’s purely an individual responsibility when it’s the benefit of our whole city if children can be raised here.

He said he would cut that program. He said he would cut Medicaid in half. I mean, times are tough as they are, and to have a gubernatorial candidate running on an agenda of, “I’m gonna make working people’s lives harder and more expensive,” I want to find the consultant who sold him that dream ’cause they must have had an incredible pitch. It makes no sense to me.

If Governor Hochul is reelected, where do you hope to take that partnership?

I would say continuing on childcare. What we have delivered funding for is enough to take a program for 2,000 2-year-olds to 12,000 2-year-olds next year. We want to deliver this for every single 2-year-old in New York City. And as of now, we’re scheduled to expand to all of the Bronx, all of Staten Island.

We want it to be every single borough, every single 2-year-old, and the governor has said she’s committed to the expansion of this program. To me, when we’re talking about a cost-of-living crisis, we’re talking about the most expensive city in America. Childcare is the second leading expense for working families in the city. If we can deliver that, what we are really delivering to New Yorkers is a more affordable life. That has to be the job.

Talk to me about the Democratic Socialists of America. Your name has become synonymous in many ways with that movement. It has been one of the dominant political stories of the last year, this rise of DSA candidates winning races across the country. Why do you think now is the time for that organization? Why not five years ago? Why not 10 years ago? Why not five years from now?

I think precisely because the movement is built around delivering dignity to working-class people. Today’s politics is an illustration of the betrayal of the working class. Never before has there been such an urgent demand for a new kind of politics. Here in New York City, the problems that working-class people are facing are in many ways the problems that working-class people are facing across the country: an inability to afford their rent, their childcare, their groceries, their electricity bills.

So that message of fighting for working-class Americans, it’s compelling wherever you are. That’s what drew me to DSA in the first place, was that this was an entire organization built around an understanding that this had to be the focus of our politics. That politics had to mean material wins for working-class people, and that we had to be willing to fight for it.

One of the things that I really love so much about what it means to be a DSA member is the D stands for “democratic.” The organization does what its members decide to do. I think in a lot of politics it feels like there’s the set of people who make the decisions, and there’s everybody else who has to go along with them.

The whole point of this is democracy, that people should be able to choose their own future. People should be able to not just choose their own leaders but also take that democracy and extend it from the ballot box to the rest of their lives.

On that note, we’ve been doing a lot of coverage at WIRED of data centers. I would be curious to hear your point of view on the data center movement, and why you think that specific issue has become such a flashpoint in this election. Where do you think that comes from?

I think the movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.

Because it shows the ways in which this fight is cutting across the typical lines that separate Americans. It’s a bipartisan fight. Me and Ron DeSantis don’t have much in common, and yet there is a similar opposition to the development of these kinds of data centers.

It speaks to a few things. Think about the incredible amount of energy that we are talking about when we’re talking about AI. You think about the version of ChatGPT; just the training of that model took the same amount of energy it would take to power all of San Francisco for three days.

That’s the scale. So what you’re seeing in opposition from Americans across the country is an opposition for what these data centers would mean in their day-to-day lives, what it would mean in their electricity rates, what it would mean in terms of the impact on their environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been a governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: our risk, their reward.

You’re seeing it whether you’re in Florida, whether you're in New York, across the entire country. Even in California we’ve seen municipalities that have started to ban the construction of data centers entirely.

You’ve supported New York state setting a one-year pause on data center construction. What next?

One of the solves is a recognition of the costs that come with AI. So much of what we are talking about is based on a very limited amount of information that we have. That is by design, because when we’re talking about these incredibly powerful companies, we also are talking about a level of opacity that renders it almost impossible for us to make an informed conclusion as to how much this query is actually costing us as a society.

Do you mean an absence of data about energy use? Or do you mean the idea that this technology is talked about as mythical rather than infrastructure?

I mean the former. I think that, frankly, there’s an attempt to make this technology seem as if it is mythical or as if it is divine.

There is a real investment in the idea that this is so complicated that the only rational response should be that we trust those who created it.

In many ways, it’s what Facebook was arguing in 2008, that they should be able to regulate themselves. Yet what we need to see is a response that grasps the scale of the adoption of this technology and the incentives that are driving a lot of this technology at this time, and the fact that we are now at a point where there are far too many similarities between the housing bubble and the state of AI in our economy today.

Do you trust the Sam Altmans of the world?

No. Do you trust the Sam Altmans of the world?

But no, I don’t. In the context of AI, you focus obviously on New York. What is your role in shaping how AI affects New Yorkers?

It’s a role on a practical level. I also think it’s a role that reckons with the enormity of AI’s impact. Now, on the practical level, it means formulating one of the most comprehensive AI moratoriums in any American school system, which we put forward, that would ban the use of generative AI for students from 2K through eighth grade.

Ban it because we need students to be given the room to be students. Students to be able to try and fail and learn, and also to bring an end to the use of our students as guinea pigs for the profit motives of technology companies. There’s been this strange thing over the last few years, maybe last few decades: While we would not be willing to have a pharmaceutical company help write the curriculum of a science class, we have been all too willing to partner with technology companies to not just inform the products that are used in the classroom, but also how they are taught.

Then, to the second point, the fact that the impact of AI is not purely an economic impact or an ecological impact, it is also an emotional impact. For all of the focus on job numbers and what jobs will be replaced by AI, there also has to be a reckoning with job satisfaction. There are a lot of jobs where the very purpose of the job is starting to be stripped away by artificial intelligence. There was recently an interview that The Daily conducted with a mathematics professor.

In tears, speaking about AI’s newfound ability to solve this age-old problem that inspired a crisis for him and for other mathematicians as to what they were doing now. What purpose did they have?

I think that is a question that should be at the forefront of how we respond to AI, because for too long, we’ve treated it, in your language, as a mythical thing, as an unknowable thing. In fact, it is a thing very much within human control. That means that we have to answer these questions, thinking about humanity as the primary responsibility.

You’ve said that citywide AI policy has been guided by the question of what we can do in the face of a complete abdication of federal law. How does that affect your ability to rein in the technology on a municipal level? How would you like to see the federal government handling this technology right now?

I would like to see them reckon with the questions of the similarities between the housing bubble and the nature of AI in the economy today. I would like to see them reckon with the wildly varying estimates of actual profitability of these companies, and the ways in which so much of their business dealings are attempts at continuing to prop up a completely artificial valuation of themselves that justifies the amount of money that they’re spending on a daily basis.

I would like to see them reckon with the fact that the application of AI has already been seen to have fatal consequences. When we’re talking about AI hallucinations, this is not just of intellectual interest. It’s also something that almost led us to war with China. When we’re talking about AI’s use of outdated information, that’s what led to our government bombing an Iranian children’s school.

This is right now. This is not a hypothetical future. What we’re doing here in New York City is we’re looking to utilize every tool we have in the face of that abdication. Some of those tools are very practical. It’s the implementation of a new rule by our Department of Consumer and Worker Protection that realtors cannot use AI-generated images of apartments.

They looked incredible, but they were not real.

The housing market is tough enough. You don't need to wonder if your dream apartment is actually a dream. You should know that it is something that exists.

Similarly, a lot of New Yorkers have been trapped in these doom loops with chatbots, so we’ve put together another rule that puts a limitation on that.

These are the kinds of day-to-day actions we can take. What we are talking about is something of international importance, and yet all too often when it is raised at that level, it is caricatured as: Everything that we’re doing is critically important because we are in a race with China. That kind of arms race terminology is used to justify every abdication of duty in this country.

You have a bafflingly good relationship with President Trump. Have you talked to him about AI?

We’ve had conversations about a lot of different topics that affect the city.

Do you feel confident in his administration’s ability to get a handle on that technology?

I think that federal policy has been lacking thus far on this, and I think that the critiques that I’ve just leveled, that is how I honestly feel about what federal policy has been thus far.

WIRED has reported extensively this year on the surveillance tech at Madison Square Garden. We’ve described it as a panopticon, among other things. We’ve published several stories about this. We’re actually being sued by James Dolan over that reporting.

I want to know what you think about what is happening there, and I’m curious about your view on whether a private citizen, someone like James Dolan, should be able to wield that kind of surveillance power over everyday New Yorkers.

No. I don't think that should be allowed. I think that it is indicative of much that is wrong in our country today in terms of the use of technology.

How does one, say the mayor of New York City, address something like that?

I think first they would do it in a WIRED interview, and then there is also legislation that City Council member Shahana Hanif has introduced, and I think that that’s an important response to this kind of an issue.

It’s an issue that has frankly been true not just at Madison Square Garden. I think also at Radio City Music Hall, where I think there was at one time reporting of a mother who is a lawyer taking her child to see a show and then being barred from entering because of her professional work.

Last year I asked you if technology was making democracy stronger or weaker. You told me weaker. What about today?

I have family members sending AI videos of me, to me, thinking that it’s real. I have a family member who complimented me on a 45-minute debate that I had with a European member of parliament. And I watched the video, I was like, “This is not me.”

I could not last through that video. Apparently, I did well. Defeated my European AI counterpart. But it wasn’t real. And I think that there is a real crisis of faith as to what is real right now, and some of the application of it is lighthearted, it’s funny, but it is quite terrifying to think that in an age of such little faith in traditional institutions, how even that could be diminished further by the application of this technology in that way.

We need to close by talking about the future. The Democratic Party is going through a lot of change right now. Let’s fast-forward, say, a decade. It’s 2036. What do you hope the party looks like, and who’s running it?

I hope that party looks like one that realizes the only majority in this country is the working class, and that it fights for it, and that it understands that no longer can an ambitious version of the party only be one that we find in history books. There’s too many monuments in this city to incredible figures who showcase what it could look like to fight for working-class people. We need that to be a living, breathing politic. I think the people who run it have to be the American people.

I don’t know. Hopefully I will have finished a second term, but I can never take that for granted.

#505. The 6 best budget headphones of the year are all under $100

If you want to cheat the system a bit and get your hands on incredible, crisp sound from a pair of headphones under $100, we've got you. You no longer need to choose between a cheap pair of headphones and incredible features like active noise cancellation, Hi-Res Audio certification, and multi-device pairing.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Sure, you might have your eyes on the class-leading Sony WH-1000xM6 headphones, but they'll cost you $450. It's not necessary to dish out that much money when you can get headphones for a fraction of the price (with much of the same functionality) or, better yet, noise-cancelling headphones that carry longer battery life and a stronger sonic punch than the AirPods Max.

All this to say, cheap headphones can be genuinely great headphones — if you know where to look. That's why we've tested a bunch of picks under $100 to find the best budget headphones available. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

If you're still an Apple loyalist when it comes to headphones, stick with us for a sec. You'll soon discover that these top picks from popular budget audio brands like JLab, Anker, and JBL are giving the market’s best a run for their money. We even have a bargain entry from Sony that’s well worth a look.

Don't believe it? You'll want to see for yourself by reading our reviews of the best headphones under $100 below.

It's hard to find a better value pair of headphones than the JLab JBuds Lux ANC, especially on sale. During Black Friday 2025, we saw them drop all the way down to $27.99, but we've also caught them on sale just under $40 and $50 year-round. For balanced sound and adjustable ANC, that's an absolute steal.

Lead Shopping Reporter Bethany Allard tried out these headphones and came away with the take that they're the Bose QuietComfort headphones made affordable. Their sound profile is relatively balanced out of the box, but even better after some adjusting with the equalizer in the app. The ANC is solid, especially for their price point, and with the app, can also be adjusted to different levels (which isn't even a given on more premium headphones like the QuietComforts).

Their design also invokes the more expensive headphones, offering a standard look in a nice array of colorways. Senior Shopping Reporter Haley Henschel owns these headphones herself and especially appreciates the long-wear comfort they provide (Allard found them a little uncomfortable after a few hours of wear, so this can vary from person to person). Still, undeniably, their 40-hour battery life also allows for extended wear time, making them an especially great option for anyone who travels frequently or likes to wear over-ear headphones while they work.

Retailing at $49.95, the price tag on these JBL Tune 510BT headphones is kind of unbeatable, making them ideal for those who are trying to save money. Don't expect them to perform magical acts for you, but also don't underestimate this handy JBL pair. They're great if you're not devoted enough of an audiophile to consider professional-level sound quality (or lack thereof) a dealbreaker.

The Tune 510BT headphones do everything wireless headphones are supposed to: They provide reasonably good sound quality, allow you to switch between two device audio outputs at once, and last for days on end. Each of these points comes with a caveat — to be expected when your headphones come out costing less than 50 bucks.

As for sound quality, these JBLs won't provide active noise cancellation (though their ear cups certainly protect your ears from hearing what goes on in the outside environment). That being said, you'll still hear a bit of outside noise mixed with your favorite song.

When testing out the multi-device connection of this JBL model, we found that it was possible but worked in a much slower fashion than its counterparts. In other words, when stopping a video on YouTube and immediately launching into a song on the phone, the headphones didn't immediately reflect this switch: It took them a good three to four seconds to start playing the second audio input.

In terms of battery life, we were impressed with the fact that these headphones were fully drained only after 38 hours — which comes quite close to JBL's promise of a 40-hour battery life. The device gave off a little tone that signified the battery was almost out, but this feature (in a real-life versus for-testing-only setting) is honestly "too little, too late." Unlike in other headphone models, there unfortunately wasn't a voice that announced the exact battery percentage when powering on the Tune 510BTs. To make up for this small flaw, the headphones are equipped with Quick Charge functionality. Just five minutes of them being plugged in via a USB-C connection adds two hours of power. Pretty sweet.

These headphones are massive — reminiscent of a gaming headset (think wide and deep ear cups, a thick band, and an undeniable heaviness). That being said, they certainly aren’t meant for working out (especially not running), unless you don't mind wearing something clunky and heavy on your head while boosting those endorphins. If you're planning on wearing them around the house, on a long plane ride, or during your daily gaming ritual, you'll fall in love with these budget headphones. After all, nothing about them screams "budget" and they're super new on the market.

Despite their cumbersome frame, these headphones take “accommodation” to the next level with a floating axis design, rotating ear cups, and a cozy plush headband.

The Space One outclass their rivals in two key areas. The first is (and don't laugh) the fact that they come with a cute, color-coordinated carrying bag. The second is that five quick minutes of charging boosts the power of these headphones not by one hour, not by two hours, but by four whole hours. They also have three mics with an AI algorithm that pinpoints your voice and amplifies it on calls. In case you don't want to hear the voices of others, they are specially designed to reduce crowd noise by up to 98 percent.

In terms of how this crowd noise reduction feature fared in real-time, I would say that the passive noise cancellation aspect of the headphones was more responsible for making it feel like you're in your own musical bubble than the ANC. We still recommend trying the adaptive noise cancellation feature since it adequately adjusts noise reduction to your surroundings. You’ll get to enjoy the full-bodied sound that blasts from Anker’s 40mm dynamic drivers with minimal interference.

The (completely free) Soundcore app is chock-full of add-on features that you can enable at your convenience. One of these is currently in beta testing — it's called Easy Chat and lowers your music volume when it detects speech. While this is theoretically good for calls (no more scrambling to turn off your rap/hip-hop song queue when grandma calls to check in), I once started to sing along to a song, which sadly turned off, thanks to this feature being enabled. Bear that in mind when toying with all of Soundcore's fancy audio tools.

If you don't need all the bells and whistles that come with top-of-the-line headphones, the Sony WH-CH520 will likely check your must-have boxes. To be completely frank, these Sonys look akin to headsets given out on flights — what with their primitive earpads, basic head cushion band, and inability to completely fold into themselves to save space. Yet, functionality sometimes trumps appearances, and this sentiment rings true for the WH-CH520 model.

Sony's WH-CH520 headphones are a great pair of affordable, basic headphones. They'd be nice for working out or sitting in the office. And they come in stylish colors like butter yellow and pink.

Through the compatible Sony app, you can manage connected devices, play around with the sound equalizer, set up "360 Reality Audio" by analyzing your ear shape, and choose whether you want to prioritize sound quality or stable connection. The learning curve to figuring out the headphones' on-ear controls is not steep at all: Press the "+" button twice to skip forward a song, the "-" button twice to go back, and the power button to start or stop.

Beware — the headphones' ear cups are kind of tiny, which can provide an uncomfortable experience for those whose ears are on the larger side. They're meant to sit on top of your ears, rather than enclose them like over-ear headphones. As far as durability goes, we could only infer that snapping the headphones' band in two would be an easy task, since this pair felt quite flimsy overall and wasn't all too cushioned. Still, the audio quality of this Sony pair certainly packed a punch. When running in them (pretty comfortable, all things considered), the sound of traffic and the wind was just barely audible — certainly way less audible than you'd expect from such a minimalistic headphone design.

Sometimes you just want headphones that require very little charging when necessary, and the Wave Pro fit that description to a T. We’re talking nearly three times the amount of battery life as the market’s top-selling models, plus some of the strongest quick charging available. Not to mention, they sound great.

Other models on this list may provide longer charges, but the Wave Pro have the most accurate battery life ratings. A full charge generates between 50 to 55 hours of noise-cancelling use and 75 to 80 hours when disabling the feature. Our unit averages a recharge once a month.

The combination of 40mm DLC dynamic drivers, Hi-Res Audio certification, and LDAC creates resonant sound that streams at three times the bitrate of standard codecs. Bass is robust on contemporary tracks, while vocals are striking on ballads and live performances. EarFun’s adjustable 10-band EQ leaves room to tweak the soundstage to your liking, though it’s best to stick with the default settings. Turning on ANC will tune out a high number of disruptive sounds. Music sounds just as good in ambient mode; you can hear what’s happening in proximity loudly and clearly, and it won’t affect playback.

Design-wise, the Wave Pro are constructed better than, I'd say, 90 percent of similarly priced competitors. Their all-plastic frame with plush leather earpads and headband supplies enough comfort and protection for long-term use.

Even if the call quality and controls leave much to be desired, the Wave Pro make up for these shortcomings with their prominent hallmarks.

We highly recommend the Major IV to brand enthusiasts who love Marshall’s legacy audio and minimalist retro aesthetic. Those are two heritage traits that the brand always knocks out of the park, and this modern wireless audio release is no different.

Besides their markdown in price (down to $100 from $150), the Major IV put on an audio clinic. These headphones sound articulate, clean, and engaging. Depth and nuance are noticeable from the moment you press play. There is no need for sound customization, which is great considering the headphones lack the settings to do so.

Marshall’s ingenuity is well demonstrated through its physical controls. Look at the gold-plated multi-directional knob that allows for seamless operation (call management, device pairing, playback, voice activation). Its solid tactility ensures that users' intended commands are met. The other feature that gives these old school-looking cans some ultramodern swagger is wireless charging. Say what? Yes, these headphones work with Qi-compatible chargers to power up without being tethered to a USB-C cable. I have not seen this on any other pair of headphones. Up to 80 hours of playtime is another major selling point.

Complaints can be made about the Major IV’s discomfort and poor noise isolation. Those are the compromises you’ll have to deal with for professional sound performance.

Check out our review of the updated Marshall Major V.

In case we weren't clear enough before, cheaper does not mean worse by any means (and vice versa) when it comes to headphones. Not always, at least.

Yet, the general trend still stands that the "higher-end" a pair of headphones is, the more likely you are to get better sound quality (aka undistorted bass), more playtime, and state-of-the-art features like adaptive ANC.

Budget headphones are known to leak sound more often than their pricier alternatives, and they'll likely have fewer extras, like spatial audio for immersive 3D sound and TalkThru technology (which amplifies your convo buddy's voice while reducing music volume instantly) featured in some of JBL’s flagship headphones.

Nonetheless, we made it our mission to find headphones — both on-ear and over-ear models — that aren't "higher-end" in price and borrow a lot of standout functionality from their more expensive counterparts.

The simple-and-sweet answer to this question is "Bluetooth." When you don't want dangling wires interfering with your music listening experience (unless you're a TikTok girly who wants to intentionally flaunt the wires on walks), Bluetooth comes in to save the day — by providing your headphones with seamless cross-device compatibility. According to PCMag, "wireless no longer means poor sound and battery life." Bluetooth headphones "still compress hi-res audio, but... preserve quality much better than in the past, and battery life has steadily improved with each new generation." Upon setting up your newest headphones purchase, you'll be prompted to connect to a device via Bluetooth. The whole process should only take you about 5 seconds. Simplicity, after all, is key.

Think of it as the real-life definition of "headphones on, world off." Active noise cancellation achieves the effect of tuning out your surroundings by using mics that capture exterior noises. Then, "audio processing circuitry... takes those noises and generates their inverse to cancel them out in real-time," as PCMag explained.

PS: There's also something called passive noise cancellation. It uses physical engineering to manually insulate your ears. Most earbuds and over-ear headphones already have this kind of noise cancellation handy — arising from the sheer shape of the earplug tips that fit snugly into your ear or the way over-ear cups create a seal that blocks off extraneous sound.

Not all of the headphones we tested boast ANC, but those that do allow you to turn on what's called transparency mode, which is a fancy way of saying you'll be able to hear your surroundings if you choose. Sometimes, you can even manipulate just how much of the outside world you want within (literal) earshot. This feature proves super helpful for city dwellers who don't want to get hit by a car while blasting "Empire State of Mind" at full volume.

To bring you this list of the very best under-$100 wireless headphones, we rigorously tested headphones over three to four weeks. While testing, we considered:

The selections on this lift were driven first by price, as we wanted the options here to be truly affordable. Everything on this list is under $100, and we tested if the value matched the price.

We tested these earbuds with various songs, from live performances to bass-heavy electronic music, R&B, rock, and folksy guitar songs. We evaluated how they sounded out of the box, along with any EQ presets or custom controls.

This variable revolved around the aesthetic feel of each tested item, how comfortable it was during wear, and how well it was able to withstand daily use. We assessed whether their features translated to unnecessary bulk and whether they were travel-friendly (could fold into a tight bundle, came with a case, etc.).

With wireless headphones, you have to rely on a battery charge, so we considered which headphones will last multiple wears without needing recharged.

Stacia Datskovska is an NYU journalism major (graduating this December). Her work has appeared in USA Today, Boston Globe, Teen Vogue, HuffPost, Bustle, and more. When she's not writing something or other, Stacia can be spotted crying over poetry, making a home-cooked meal, or walking on an NYC pier. For her more half-baked thoughts: @staciadats on Twitter.

#501. ICE Is Inspiring Latinos to Vote in Historic Numbers

Civil society groups have feared that the mass anti-immigration surges across the US this year would have a chilling effect on voter turnout in Latino communities.

In reality, they have had the opposite result.

”We have not seen here at the local level people worried to show up to vote because they think ICE is going to be there,” Michael Mireles, a canvassing organizer with LUPE Votes, a get-out-the-vote group in southern Texas, tells WIRED. “People are driven right now by their anti-ICE sentiment, and it's not stopping them from going to the polls.”

Mireles is one of a dozen activists, volunteers, and organizers WIRED spoke to in recent weeks about the impact Trump’s hard-line immigration policies were having on communities that turned out in surprising numbers for the president in 2024. Trump’s immigration policies have disproportionately targeted Latino neighborhoods, and many law-abiding US citizens have been caught up in the ICE dragnet. For weeks now, the Department of Homeland Security and the Trump administration have claimed that they have no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on election day, but President Donald Trump and administration officials like DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin and attorney general Todd Blanche have repeatedly hinted at some sort of deployment.

While there is certainly still fear about what may happen on Election Day, the overwhelming message coming from the Latino community is that rather than being cowed, they are defying the administration to turn up in record numbers.

These experiences are backed up by data. Early voting figures indicate people are casting their ballots at a much higher rate than in recent elections. By Monday afternoon, more than 57million people had voted early, 10 million more than the total early voting figure in the 2022 midterms. In many states, Latino communities are accounting for a larger share than in previous years, according to data from the University of Florida’s Election Lab.

In Texas, there have already been over 400,000 people who didn’t vote in 2024 who have cast their ballot in 2026. Of that figure, 50 percent are Latino voters, Tom Bonier, a Democrat strategist and adviser to data company TargetSmart, revealed in an interview last week.

And what’s happening in Texas is being replicated across the country, according to data from TargetSmart. By October 27, 3.8 million Hispanic and Latino voters had cast a ballot nationwide, a massive increase from the 2.35 million Hispanic and Latino voters who had voted by the same date in 2022.

“Where large Hispanic communities exist in Texas, there is elevated turnout even above the blistering statewide pace,” Michael McDonald, who runs the University of Florida Election Lab, wrote in an analysis last week. “Texas Hispanics are voting at higher levels than in past elections, as we can see in Florida, Georgia, and North Carolina.”

This analysis was backed up by data shared with WIRED by the League of United Latin American Citizens, the largest Latino civil rights group in the country.

The league’s data shows that in Texas’ 15th congressional district, which includes a part of the Rio Grande Valley, over 12,000 people who have voted early did not vote in the previous elections. Those votes could have a significant impact in a district where incumbent Republican congresswoman Monica De La Cruz won in 2022 by around 12,000 votes.

Dozens of organizations and individuals across the country have worked tirelessly for months to convince these communities that they need to stand up and have their voice heard, and the best way to do that is to vote.

“We didn't try to pacify people or make it seem like it wasn't going to be that bad,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with 614 ICE Watch and Ohio Good Neighbor Network tells WIRED. “We didn't want to exaggerate either. We said this is the reality of what's been happening. These are examples of what we've seen. You've told us that it's really bad and that you don't want this to continue, so you have a choice. You're either going to show up and vote and make sure that your voice is counted, or you're going to stay home and continue to deal with this for the next two or three years, possibly longer. I really think that motivated a lot of people.”

The experiences of citizens who have faced down ICE’s massive surges have played a huge factor.

“Folks in these places that have really come face-to-face with some of the worst of the ICE violence are feeling like they understand that preparation is key,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, a group that combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They understand how traumatizing this is, how chaotic it is. I think they want to be as prepared as possible for any scenario.”

But Garvey says that facing down ICE already means these communities are “frankly, a little less scared. They have faced this already, and it's scary, but they also know that it's possible, and that the escalation can happen very, very quickly.”

Living United for Change in Arizona is a group that targets working-class Latino voters with its get-out-the-vote efforts. In one recent week, volunteers knocked on thousands of doors, César Fierros, a spokesperson for the group tells WIRED. 1,000 people told the group they voted early or mailed their ballots back. “That's a really good sign; that's something that we have really never seen before,” Fierros says. “People are saying ‘Yes, there are threats out there, looming, but we're still going to show up regardless.”

In DeKalb County in Georgia, volunteers from the Save America Movement, an anti-Trump group, heard similar messages from people streaming into early polling locations earlier this month.

“We’re hearing it everywhere our Vote Safe team members are,” Mary Corcoran, cofounder and executive director of the Save America Movement, tells WIRED. “Voters came through in a steady stream from the moment the polls opened until they closed. Person after person told our team that nothing was going to keep them from voting this year. People know what this administration is trying to do, and they are refusing to be scared out of their own democracy.”

In Nevada, secretary of state Cisco Aguilar, who is running for reelection against election denier Jim Marchant, believes that in order to convince reticent voters to show up, elected leaders need to “get real.”

“I did a Latino community event [and said] we have to actually fucking vote to tell these motherfuckers to fuck off,” Aguilar tells WIRED. “And when you get real with them about that, and they know that you're willing to stand up and fight for them, then they are willing to consider showing up to vote.”

This is a sentiment echoed by Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states with voting rights group Common Cause, who says it’s important to “lean into that defiance” and tell voters “that the opposition wouldn't be making it so difficult if there wasn't power in voting.”

“The threats are real, but so is the joy, and there is a real joy that comes in participating in democracy,” Almeida says.
