#499. Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed

DETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.

Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs.

"At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jonathan Dankenbring, Rivian senior manager of prototype manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."

Also known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.

Printers can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.

Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.

Dankenbring said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours.

"It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Dankenbring said.

The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.

"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Dankenbring said.

Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.

There's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors, which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.

Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.

"By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."

Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.

Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.

Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost.

Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.

"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.

Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.

GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.

The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.

Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing.

"The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Jonathan Dankenbring is Rivian's senior manager of prototype manufacturing. A previous version of this article misidentified him.

#497. Apple AirPods 5 Review: Better Than Before but Not Quite Pro

I’ve owned AirPods since the original pair launched in 2016. Over the years, I’ve tested earbuds from many brands, but I always come back to my trusty AirPods. They’re easy to pair, they integrate well with the Apple ecosystem, and they deliver some of the best-sounding active noise cancellation (ANC) on the market. The latest AirPods 5 continue the trend and deliver more of Apple’s best audio features at a lower price than their predecessor.

The AirPods 5 come in two models: $129 with a standard case and $149 with a wireless charging case that works with Apple Watch chargers, Qi-compatible chargers, and USB-C. Both include ANC, which is a welcome change from the AirPods 4, where you had to pay extra ($179) for the privilege of a feature that’s increasingly standard on most wireless earbuds.

For $149, the AirPods 5 (with a wireless charging case) are an easy recommendation. But after a month of testing, I’d still pay extra to get the AirPods Pro 3. The difference comes down to noise cancellation, fit, and controls.

First and foremost, if you’re buying the AirPods 5, spend the extra $20 on the version with a wireless charging case. You’ll get an extra hour of battery life (up to five hours) on the earbuds and an extra two (up to 22 hours) with the charging case compared to the $129 model. That's the same battery life as the AirPods 4 without ANC, so you’re actually getting more listening time even with noise cancellation.

Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case

The inclusion of ANC in both AirPods 5 models is the biggest upgrade here. You no longer have to pay extra just to get noise cancellation, and even the $129 model is a better deal than the standard AirPods 4 were at launch. Both versions also support Conversation Awareness, Live Translation, and Spatial Audio, along with Apple’s Siri features.

And, for semi-open earbuds, the AirPods 5 have exceptional ANC. Apple says the noise cancellation removes up to 50 percent more external noise than the AirPods 4 with ANC, due to a redesigned multi-port acoustic architecture and improved audio processing. I can’t verify that percentage, but the improvement was noticeable during my testing.

I was especially impressed on a domestic flight, where the AirPods 5 did a stellar job at suppressing the sound of the airplane engines. They didn’t make the cabin totally disappear, and the AirPods Pro 3 still deliver stronger isolation, but it was a huge improvement compared to the AirPods 4 with ANC.

Transparency mode sounds even more natural. I found this especially useful with Adaptive Audio, which automatically balances ANC with Transparency mode based on your surroundings. On a run, for example, footsteps approaching from behind prompted the earbuds to lower my music and let more environmental sound through. The transition felt smooth enough that the outside noise almost blended into the song. I could stay aware of my surroundings without getting distracted by every little thing happening around me.

For people who run outdoors or commute, the open-ear design can be more appealing than the tighter seal of the Pros. You sacrifice some isolation, but you get a more natural sense of what’s happening around you.

The notable improvements can't overcome the simple fact that I generally prefer the silicone tips of the AirPods Pro 3 to the semi-open fit of the AirPods 5. The AirPods Pro 3 create a snug seal without making my ears feel clogged, and the interchangeable sizes let me tailor the fit. That seal also makes a noticeable difference when I’m working out. During longer runs, I found the AirPods 5 could start slipping as sweat built up. The Pros stayed put. Their more secure fit also naturally improves noise cancellation.

Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case

The AirPods 5 inherit the Pro 3’s volume controls, which let you adjust the volume by swiping up or down on the stem, but I’ve found the feature tricky to use across AirPods models because the stems are so short and slim that I struggle to get the right touch with my long nails. I generally prefer the volume controls on Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds, which offer more surface area to work with.

I find the Pro 3’s controls are easier to use than the AirPods 5’s, especially while running. The stem protrudes a little more where it meets the earbud, giving me a more accessible spot to press. With AirPods 5, I’ve had to take an earbud out just to locate the right control spot, which is not ideal mid-run. A few days ago, I nearly sacrificed one to Lake Michigan after fumbling with it. The upgraded IP57 rating means the earbuds can withstand brief immersion in water, but I wouldn’t recommend testing that claim in a lake.

While the AirPods 5 offer a lot for the money, the pinpoint controls and a few missing features make the Pro 3 worth the splurge in my mind. The Pros have integrated heart-rate sensing for workouts, hearing aid features, and longer battery life with ANC enabled.

The $100 price difference between the two is significant, though. For casual listeners, tweens, and teens, the AirPods 5 are great. You still get solid noise cancellation, Apple’s seamless ecosystem integration, and an open-ear design that’s more comfortable for people who don’t like silicone eartips. The smaller charging case is another perk—it slips more naturally into a pocket or the waistband of leggings.

But as an iPhone owner who works out daily and travels frequently, I’d still spend $249 on the AirPods Pro 3. Their secure fit, stronger noise cancellation, and more accessible controls make them the better all-around earbuds for me.

The AirPods 5 are the better value. The AirPods Pro 3 are the better earbuds.

#496. Election Day 2026: Find when polls open, close, and other voting details

The Nov. 3 midterm elections are here, and the outcome will determine the makeup of Congress and the trajectory of President Donald Trump's remaining years in office.

So if you haven't already voted, still need to mail in a ballot, or don't even know where to start, the hours are counting down. For an overview of voting deadlines, drop box and polling locations, and registration information, visit Vote.org, USA.gov, or keep reading below.

More than 51 million Americans have already voted in the 2026 midterm elections. The number of people voting by mail grew substantially in 2020, and eight states now host what are known as all-mail elections or offer universal mail-in voting.

Mail ballots are sent early, with most states requiring at least a week's lead time before Nov. 3. If you were issued an absentee or mail ballot and plan to send it by mail, your ballot must be postmarked by or on election day, not after. A late postmark can void your ballot. If you never received your ballot, contact your election office ASAP.

In some states, voters can also drop off their ballots at designated drop boxes (the websites of county registrars typically list drop box locations, such as the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder). Around 15 states require drop box options for voters, many located at places like libraries and parks:

Another 11 states prohibit drop boxes, so make sure your ballot gets postmarked if you are registered in these states:

To find more rules on drop box voting, absentee voting, and voting by mail, visit your state's registrar of voters or scroll down to the state-by-state database on Vote.org.

Despite a growing number of voters skipping the polls in favor of mail, many voters still cast their ballot in person. Voters are assigned to an in-person polling location based on the address they used to register to vote, and most can start voting before Nov. 3.

Polling times vary by state, with some states offering in-person voting as early as one month before election day (this practice is usually referred to as early in-person voting). Voters with disabilities may need to go to a different polling location, depending on their accommodation needs.

Voters do not need any special equipment or documents to cast their vote. You may need to bring a form of verification to the polls, however, depending on your state. Scroll down for more information.

Voters are also allowed to bring in personal notes, a voter's guide, and even sample ballots into the polling booth.

Voters can find out their nearest polling location by checking their registration or calling their local registrar of voters. They can also use an online polling locator such Vote.org or the National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS).

That depends on your state. Voter ID laws vary across the country, so check with your state election officials to be sure. In some cases, you may still be able to vote without an ID by signing an identity form.

Can I track my ballot if I voted by mail?

Yes. Most states offer some form of ballot tracking for voters. Find specific information on ballot tracking via your state's registrar website or call 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683).

Yes and no. Ballots can't be challenged without a real legal basis under the National Voter Registration Act. A voter purge, in which election workers "clean up" voter databases by deleting names, can't be conducted within 90 days of a federal election. If you were on the roll as of August, filled out your ballot correctly and on time, your vote should count.

Federal agents and law enforcement cannot legally seize voting machines, nullify ballots, or stop the count.

That being said, groups may still challenge swaths of ballots up until the election. If your registration is challenged at the polls, you can still cast a provisional ballot.

Electronic voting apparatuses are overseen by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC) and thousands of election officials to ensure their safety and reliability. While recent studies have uncovered security flaws, election security researchers say they have not yet led to any kind of election interference, as suggested by some critics and conspiracy theorists.

Instead, experts suggest the biggest threat to election integrity is the spread of misinformation, which is increasingly enabled by AI.

Can the president intervene in the election?

The administration has been casting doubt on the legitimacy of the midterm results, including claims that thousands of noncitizens are casting votes in this year's election. The majority of noncitizen voters charged with crimes have been found to be lawful residents.

Despite threats from the Trump administration, the president cannot issue an executive order or harness emergency powers to take over or nationalize the election process. Previous executive orders attempting to change the electoral process have been struck down or blocked by courts, and additional safeguards prevent the current Congress from refusing to seat newly elected officials.

#494. The Endlessly Meme-able Steve Kornacki Is Not a Meme Person

Standing in front of a gigantic map isn’t a traditional path to fame. But in 2020, during the presidential face-off between Donald Trump and Joe Biden, Steve Kornacki became America’s sweetheart for his enthusiastic delivery of state-by-state election results. The NBC data analyst gracefully guided teeth-grinding, fist-clenching viewers through Biden’s eventual victory, and the rest is history: That same year, Kornacki was named one of People’s sexiest men alive; the internet became obsessed with his khaki pants; and he earned the nicknames “chartthrob” and “map daddy.”

Kornacki further established himself as the king of election season with the “Kornacki Cam” during 2026 midterm primary election nights, when his nonstop behind-the-scenes livestreams amassed 42 million views. Now that midterm election day is upon us, Kornacki is acutely aware of how many viewers have come to rely on him. “I get very anxious about being prepared for election night,” he says, “and then thinking of all the things that I might not be prepared for, and then just taking the phone out and trying to get prepared.”

For someone who spends a lot of time logged on, Kornacki doesn’t exactly have the habits of someone who is chronically online. He seems to know nothing at all about memes, FaceTime really isn’t his thing, and he isn’t quite sure what a subreddit is. Ask him about who’s most likely to win today’s races, though, and he’ll have no shortage of knowledge to share.

#493. Germany's Gen Z protests disrupted by violence on Saturday

Nationwide protests led by young people were largely peaceful throughout the day, but reports about looting and rioting in the evening, especially in Frankfurt, overshadowed the spirit of the demonstrations.

This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31 and November 1, 2026.

The Gen Z protests in Germany were mostly peaceful throughout the day, with tens of thousands of people having participated across big and smaller cities.

The peaceful demonstrations were overshadowed by reports about violence in some cities like Frankfurt (see below).

Hesse's state interior minister said he suspects that about 100 left-wing extremists instigated the violence in Frankurt.

There were instances of disturbances in Cologne, Hamburg and Bremen, too.

Riots, looting and attacks on police broke out in several German cities after protests by tens of thousands of young people across the country demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs and greater social justice.

The demonstrations had been largely peaceful during the day.

But serious disturbances erupted in the evening in several places.

Clashes broke out in Cologne on Saturday, with about 200 people involved in disturbances near Cologne Cathedral.

Police officers were attacked on the square outside the famous cathedral, with bottles and bicycles hurled toward them.

In a nearby side street, a window was smashed by an electric scooter thrown during the unrest, police said.

According to regional broadcaster WDR, other groups besides Gen Z demonstrators were involved in riots.

Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was deeply saddening that peaceful protests were overshadowed by "extremists who had nothing but violence in mind."

While Gen Z protests across Germany were largely peaceful during the day, clashes were reported in several cities as night fell.

German police sealed off a major shopping street in central Frankfurt on Saturday night after rioters smashed shop windows, looted stores and attacked officers following a demonstration.

Police closed Die Zeil, one of Germany's busiest shopping streets, to incoming visitors and urged bystanders to leave the area.

"Anyone not involved who is still on the Zeil can leave. Access to the Zeil is no longer possible," Frankfurt police said in a post on X and in loudspeaker announcements.

Chaotic scenes unfolded along the shopping street, where dpa journalists witnessed people breaking into stores and stealing trainers and other goods.

A specialist firearms shop was also targeted, prompting several arrests, a police spokesman said.

Police also reported attacks on officers, including attacks involving incendiary devices.

The violence erupted after police broke up a demonstration organized as part of the nationwide "Gen Z regelt" (roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge") protests.

A large contingent of officers was deployed around the Zeil, with authorities advising people to avoid the area or leave central Frankfurt.

The German protests on Saturday are a part of a wider trend that has seen members of Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, protest in several European nations.

The wave of protest was triggered by students seeking education reform in France, with the standoff erupting in violence and looting two weeks ago.

For our standalone story on protests in France today, click here.

After a day of youth protests in Germany, senior police union representative Andreas Rosskopf said that there was no widespread property damage "so far."

"The Gen Z protests have turned out to be very peaceful," Rosskopf told the daily Rhenische Post.

While confrontations were reported after the marches ended in multiple cities, the people driving the clashes were "individuals acting independently, some of whom were masked."

Rosskopf, who represents Germany's federal police, said security forces acted very decisively and forcefully when such response was appropriate.

"Security forces remain absolutely ready to prevent any further clashes in the late evening of overnight," he said.

German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations.

In Hamburg, protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon.

Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister.

Police also used a water cannon in Cologne, where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters.

In Berlin, the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants.

Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters following the Gen Z demonstration in Frankfurt, authorities said.

"One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck.

"We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said.

"They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks."

Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said

Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday.

German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education.

Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down.

The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it).

Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October.

Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires.

Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully.

But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured.

In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration.

They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire.

Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out.

Following an initial estimate of several hundred people attending the rally in central Berlin, police said that some 5,000 people were now gathered at the Brandenburg Gate. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance.

One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians.

The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands of young people have joined the demonstrations in over 30 German cities, with police reporting largely peaceful protests.

Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig,  Nuremberg, and elsehwere.

Retailers in several city centers had boarded up shop windows, particularly along luxury shopping streets, fearing unrest. Some shops were already closed for the Reformation Day public holiday.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.

Police in Cologne called off the planned "Gen Z regelt" procession after some participants covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

"The demonstration will continue as a stationary rally," a police spokeswoman told the DPA news agency. Participants would remain on the Rhine riverbank, she said, appealing for restraint.

Attendance remained below the 15,000 people registered for the demonstration. Based on advance registrations, Cologne's protest was expected to be the largest in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Police repeatedly stopped a youth protest march in Stuttgart, citing participants covering their faces and leaving the agreed route.

Officers also reported smoke devices and firecrackers before the procession began. "Be loud, but remain peaceful," a police spokeswoman urged in a video.

In other German cities, police reported a largely peaceful start to demonstrations. Authorities estimated included 2,500 participants in Freiburg, more than 1,500 in Frankfurt, 1,200 in Mainz, 1,000 in Munich and 650 in Berlin.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available.

Politicians must involve young people in decision-making or risk the youth turning away from political institutions, education researcher Nina Kolleck warned.

Their exclusion "creates the impression that there is a policy for the old, but not for the young," the University of Potsdam professor told Germany's RBB Inforadio.

Kolleck pointed to decades of underinvestment in schools and the disproportionate impact of climate change on younger generations.

She warned that populist parties could exploit the resulting political vacuum if young people's frustrations continued to go unanswered.

#487. Apple iPad Mini (2026) Review: A Dream Device, but Who Is It For?

Some thought it might be dead. Some thought it had no place in an iPhone Duo world. But the iPad Mini isn’t being put out to pasture—it’s getting a massive glow-up.

Apple’s smallest tablet has been refreshed—now in its eighth generation—and with it, nearly every aspect of the device has been upgraded. It now has an OLED screen, a faster chip, a thinner chassis, more memory, waterproofing, and much more. That all comes with a higher price, though, and raises the question of just who the iPad Mini is really for among the other choices in the iPad lineup.

I’ll come straight out with it: I love this little tablet. I’ve been using it for about a week, and I happened to take it on a short trip. The perfect time for it to really shine—and shine, it did. It was the perfect companion for long Lyft rides to the airport and wait times at my gate.

The star attraction of the new iPad Mini is its 8.5-inch display. That’s a slightly larger screen than the previous generation, yet the overall dimensions are barely bigger. But the change from IPS to OLED is what matters. It uses an OLED Super Retina XDR display, which is not the tandem OLED seen on the iPad Pro (and OLED MacBook Pro). It doesn’t have the 120-Hz refresh rate, nor is it quite as bright. It can reach 600 nits in SDR and 1,200 nits in HDR, which is 400 nits less than the iPad Pro. It’s more or less similar to the Mini-LED M6 MacBook Pro in terms of brightness, though, which is still impressive for OLED.

The iPad Mini OLED’s brightness is sufficient for most uses, even in bright lighting conditions. But you can take it to the next level by opting for a nano-texture display, which is totally worth the extra $100 it costs. (It’s the model I tested.) It’s not an antireflective coating or a matte layer; it’s actually etched into the glass. The result is a surface that almost entirely diffuses outside light without reducing the screen’s perceived brightness. Reading outside with the iPad Mini is particularly enjoyable, as the nano-texture display not only resists reflections but even gives it a paperlike crispness. This option is also available on the MacBook Pro and iPad Pro, and there’s really nothing else like it.

The iPad Mini one-ups its siblings in sharpness. Its smaller size gives it 19 percent higher pixel density than every other iPad. And yes, it really does look incredibly clear and sharp.

There’s more to it than the display. Part of the magic is how lightweight it is—barely over half a pound, and it doesn’t feel much heavier than my phone in my hand. One-handed use feels completely natural. That’s always been true of the iPad Mini, but this latest version emphasizes that even more.

Lastly, the color options have been pared down from four to just two. The lighter goldish Starlight is still available, but now there’s the introduction of the blackish, navy-blue Midnight. This is a finish carried over from the MacBook Air. The more playful Blue and Purple color options are both gone, as is Space Gray. More options are always better, but for a device that costs $700, I can see why these more professional colors make sense.

Apple has also completely redesigned the iPad Mini’s four-speaker sound system, and a couple of interesting changes are happening. As part of its process of making the device IP67 water-resistant, Apple removed the speaker grille from the sides to create a completely sealed enclosure. Instead, the tweeters sit behind two small slits on the edges of the display glass. And then bass drivers are built directly into the display. Apple calls it an Acoustic Display.

The stereo image sounds fullest when you hold the device in portrait, as long as you keep your fingers away from the display. The vibration caused by the location of the speakers isn’t terribly noticeable unless you have the volume on full blast. Overall, the audio sounds decent for a device this size, but it won’t compare well to larger devices like an iPad Air or MacBook Air. But for watching videos or the occasional movie, it suffices.

The water resistance is a first for any iPad, which is significant. You might still worry about bringing your $700 tablet poolside, but the IP67 rating means it can handle submersion for 30 minutes in about three feet of water. In comparison, iPhones have had an IP68 rating for the past eight years, meaning they can handle twice that depth for 30 minutes.

As always, it has to be said that iPads are not really designed for taking photos. That’s a bit less true with the iPad Mini, if only because it’s so easy to use one-handed. Still, I doubt you’ll use the 12-megapixel rear camera all that much, outside of the occasional document or QR code scan. It’s decent but hasn’t been changed from the previous generation. The front-facing camera, however, got a big upgrade. It’s still a 12-megapixel camera, but it has moved to the side bezel instead of the top. That location makes video calls feel more natural.

One thing the iPad Mini is still missing is Face ID. While it’s a standard iPhone feature, Apple appears to really be reserving it for only the iPad Pro. That’s a shame. This does have Touch ID built into the power button.

A number of other iPad features still apply here, though, that make the iPad Mini feel like something you could work on. It supports extended display mode, letting you connect it to an external monitor without forcing it to mirror the screen. iPadOS also now has windowing and proper cursor support. Without a keyboard, I can’t imagine you’ll use these features as much. On the other hand, the iPad Mini’s size makes it possible to type with your thumbs (like you would on a phone).

Clearly, the 2026 iPad Mini seems to have its sights set on more than just reading books and playing games. As if the OLED display and price tag weren’t already enough to give that away. Most of the demos Apple has been using to show off with the iPad Mini were more creator-focused than I expected. We’re talking running on-device AI models or creative applications.

There are three storage configurations available: 128 GB, 256 GB, and 512 GB. All come with 12 GB of unified memory, four more than the previous iPad Mini and matching the current iPad Air. You’d never know that from Apple’s own spec sheets, though, since it’s never mentioned. Regardless, it’s part of what makes the iPad Mini a more capable little tablet, whether in heavier multitasking or for on-device AI. It’s kind of absurd that this little tablet has 12 GB of memory while the MacBook Neo is stuck at 8.

The iPad Mini’s A20 Pro chip is also more powerful than the MacBook Neo’s. This is the same silicon as in the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone 18 Pro Max—with one caveat. For the first time, the storage options dictate which version of the A20 Pro chip you get. Only the 512-GB model gets the full six-core CPU and dual 16-core Neural Engines. I tested this six-core model, but the other configurations have nerfed performance, with one fewer CPU efficiency core and only a single Neural Engine.

Performance is really solid. The A20 Pro handles games quite well, and I tested several, including Oceanhorn 3, Fortnite, No Man’s Sky, and Assassin’s Creed Mirage. None of these games looked particularly nice here, with textures and effects turned down, but the iPad Mini played them smoothly at 60 frames per second. Visually, the most impressive was No Man’s Sky, which came to iOS and iPadOS just last week. It still feels amazing to play a game this dense on a mere iPad Mini. Of course, the iPad Pro with the M5 will be a substantial upgrade for gaming performance, but if you connect a mobile controller (we like the Backbone One), you’ll have a good time.

I also tried out some local AI in LM Studio. With 12 GB of onboard memory, you’re limited in what models you can use. LM Studio recommended the 4-billion parameter version of Qwen 3.5. This isn’t the kind of model that’s going to blow anyone away, but for simple tasks, it’s nice to run a text model completely locally. This is all GPU-dependent, so performance should be identical without the second Neural Engine that comes exclusively on the 512-GB model. Of course, Siri AI is now a significant part of this platform, and the iPad Mini can run all the advanced features, including the more expressive Siri voices and on-the-fly dictation.

The previous iPad Mini cost $499 when it came out (before the price increases), and that at least felt reasonable. At this new price of $699, it’s a little harder to justify. The iPad Mini has always been a luxe but niche device. It’s sized for reading books, watching movies, and playing games. It doesn’t have the same high-stakes use case as a phone or laptop, which makes that higher premium price harder to swallow.

If you want the most powerful iPad Mini as a professional tool, you’ll probably spend at least $999. Or $1,099 with the nano-texture display. That’s the same price as the MacBook Air! I get it: The iPad Mini is an entirely different device. But I’m wondering whether real professionals would at least prefer a larger display—not only for the extra screen real estate but also for keyboard support.

I will say: The iPad Mini does work remarkably well with the Apple Pencil. If I had to choose an iPad specifically for note-taking, it’d be the iPad Mini. On the other hand, illustrators will likely prefer a larger screen. Like previous versions of the iPad Mini, it’s only compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and USB-C Apple Pencil. Even for those who use tablets in the workplace as a point-of-sale system or for specialized use cases, the higher price seems hard to justify.

Is it all just a plainly disguised way of justifying the higher prices Apple is paying for memory on the backend? The cynic in me says yes. It’s not unlike the direction Apple is heading with its OLED MacBook Pro. But putting the cynicism aside, there’s real quality-of-life value being added here, especially in the form of the OLED screen, waterproofing, and extra memory. For the right person, the iPad Mini will be the perfect product. It’s a dream device for casual use, whether it’s gaming, reading, or browsing. But I’m guessing that demographic has shrunk quite a bit with this increased price.

I’m a little perplexed why Apple isn’t at least offering an 8-GB RAM model that would bring the price down more. I know it goes against the focus on Siri AI, which needs at least 12 GB, but it would at least keep the core audience that would buy an iPad Mini in the first place. It would also help create some more separation between this and the iPad Air. The iPad Mini is $150 cheaper than the iPad Air despite having an OLED screen. The iPad Air, meanwhile, has a larger 11-inch screen and is big enough to use with the Magic Keyboard. You’ll have to weigh a number of trade-offs when choosing between these two.

And with the iPhone Duo’s arrival, the iPad Mini’s size feels even less unique. Sure, the Duo costs $2,000, but it solves the iPad Mini’s main problem: convenience. As your phone, the Duo fits in your pocket, goes with you everywhere, and is far more versatile as a pocket computer. The iPad Mini is less flexible and easier to forget and leave at home. And at $699, you may wonder whether you really need that fancy OLED screen and 12 GB of RAM.

#485. DoorDash is rolling out major holiday perks: Christmas tree delivery, Black Friday deals, and more

TL;DR: DoorDash is taking over your holiday chores. You can now get Christmas trees delivered for 20% off, score up to 50% off Black Friday deals, order party catering for up to 150 people, and have a Dasher pick up unboxed retail returns from your porch for a flat $7.99 fee.

Somewhere between mapping out the gift list, planning the family dinner, and hunting for parking at the mall, holiday errands quickly turn into a marathon. This season, DoorDash wants to do the legwork for you. The app is expanding way beyond takeout with Christmas tree delivery, party catering for 150+, sub-one-hour Black Friday deals, and doorstep retail returns.

Here's a look at every major holiday feature rolling out on DoorDash, along with the fine print you need to know before checking out.

Hauling a pine tree home strapped to the roof of a car is usually the least fun part of the holidays. From Nov. 15 to Dec. 7, DoorDash lets you order real and artificial trees directly in the app from major retailers such as The Home Depot, Lowe's, Ace Hardware, Michaels, and Kohl's. By applying promo code LITMAS at checkout, you will save 20% on any order of $60 or more that includes a tree, up to a maximum savings of $20.

Keep in mind that your cart must include a tree, and the $60 minimum applies strictly before taxes, service fees, or driver tips. The code only knocks off merchandise costs; you can only use it once, and it’s delivery-only — so pickup orders and carts bundled with alcohol won't qualify.

With Dasher Returns, DoorDash eliminates the prep work, so a courier will come directly to your home to collect eligible retail purchases and return them directly to the store for on-the-spot processing.

Open the DoorDash app and check your eligible retail order history for the Dasher Returns option.

Select the items you want to send back and schedule a pickup window.

Hand the bare items directly to your Dasher when they arrive — no shipping boxes, tape, or printed labels required.

The service costs a flat fee of $7.99 per scheduled pickup, with Dashers able to arrive in as fast as 30 minutes. It applies strictly to eligible retail merchandise purchased through supported stores on DoorDash. The feature is available in select launch cities and continues to roll out nationwide through Nov. 2026.

DoorDash is turning its retail catalog into a pocket-sized digital mall, offering on-demand delivery in under an hour from brands like Ulta Beauty, Lowe's, Best Buy, Macy's, Anthropologie, GAP, Urban Outfitters, and SKIMS.

From Nov. 23 through Nov. 30, shoppers can take advantage of Black Friday discounts of up to 50% off select items, including half-off cosmetics and stocking stuffers at Ulta Beauty, and up to 40% off tools and holiday decor at Lowe's. For gift givers, DoorDash is also discounting its own digital gift cards on Thanksgiving Day (Nov. 27 only).

Head to the Holiday Hub section in the DoorDash app between Nov. 23 and Nov. 30 to browse deals across featured retailers.

Add eligible sale items from stores like Best Buy, Ulta, or Macy's to your cart for same-day doorstep delivery.

On Nov. 27, visit the digital gift card portal in the app to claim your 10% or 20% discount.

The fine print: The Nov. 27 gift card promotion has a strict $25 discount cap and is limited to one redemption per customer. Sub-one-hour delivery relies on Express delivery estimates and may vary during peak holiday volume. Alcohol deliveries to stock the bar cart are strictly for 21+ and available only in select legal markets with valid ID verification.

DoorDash isn't just for solo takeout anymore — you can now order massive party spreads for 10 to 150+ people. Whether you're hosting Friendsgiving, an office hangout, or family dinner, you can order from chains like P.F. Chang's or local favorites like Zucker's Bagels.

Deliveries come with $0 delivery fees, an on-time guarantee, and your Dasher will even help set up the food. Plus, if you hate party math, the in-app "Ask DoorDash" tool will calculate portions and build the menu for you based on your headcount and dietary restrictions.

Head to the Catering tab in the app or go to doordash.com/catering.

Pick your delivery date and time up to two weeks ahead.

Use Ask DoorDash to map out portions and build a cart of at least $200.

Drop in code TRYDDCATER50 at checkout to get 50% off (up to $150).

For a quick solo bite between stops, you can grab the $12 Meal Boxes — dishes like pasta, tacos, or grain bowls with $0 delivery and reduced fees in 20+ cities.

The TRYDDCATER50 coupon is valid from Nov. 2 to Nov. 30, for first-time catering users only. Orders must meet a $200 minimum subtotal before taxes and fees, with maximum savings of $150 (excluding taxes, service fees, driver gratuity, and alcohol).

Consumer catering is currently available in select launch markets, and the on-time guarantee refund policy applies if your eligible catering delivery arrives 20 minutes or more past the confirmed window.

If your to-do list is already getting out of hand, hand it over to a Dasher and get back to enjoying the holidays.

The company's entry into at-home baking comes as a number of restaurants turn to consumer packaged goods to boost sales in an otherwise challenging time for the industry.

Some players, such as California Pizza Kitchen and TGI Fridays, have licensed their brands for frozen foods for decades. But other restaurant chains, including Chick-fil-A and Dutch Bros, have leaned into grocery products much more recently. For smaller companies, such as Momofuku or Carbone, space on a grocery shelf helps extend brand reach and gives consumers a chance to try their food without a reservation and at a much lower cost.

Founded by Melissa Ben-Ishay in 2008, Baked by Melissa has nine permanent locations in the New York area and ships its minicupcakes nationwide.

The regional chain has garnered attention outside the city thanks to Ben-Ishay's social media presence. On TikTok, the Baked by Melissa account has more than 2.8 million followers, fueled by popular recipe videos, such as for her green goddess salad dressing. Ben-Ishay's social media stardom has led to collaborations with Ferrero and Wonder.

Baked by Melissa had discussed at-home baking products for years, but Ben-Ishay, who is also president of the company, only decided to take the plunge a year ago during a trip to Target with her two kids, she told CNBC. A spin through the baking aisle made her decide Baked by Melissa "should be here," she said.

"I love baking cake mix. I truly do. And, quite frankly, sometimes I just think it tastes better," Ben-Ishay said.

But retail moves more slowly than Baked by Melissa's usual pace.

The dessert company needed just a few days to create New York Knicks-branded minicupcakes after the team won the NBA championship in June, for example, but figuring out retail products meant "a lot of waiting and approvals and new partners," Ben-Ishay said.

Twelve months later, the cupcake mixes have arrived on store shelves, just in time for the all-important holiday season.

For Target, the next two months will be critical as the retailer tries to woo back its core customer after a disappointing holiday season last year. That prototypical Target shopper often looks a lot like Ben-Ishay.

"We started with Target because I'm a 42-year-old mom of two, and I find myself there a lot," she said.

#482. Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience

After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.

Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practicing "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."

Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.

Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.

Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

#480. Roli Has Fallen Apart—and Left Customers Holding the Bag

Roli, the company behind expressive, touch-sensitive music devices like the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed.

Although it hasn't been officially announced, Roli reportedly ousted its CEO and founder, Roland Lamb, earlier this year. Since then, Roli has all but dissolved. (In August, a new company called Instrumental Intelligence was registered with the UK government under Lamb's name, a potential move by the founder to acquire Roli's assets).

On Monday, Roli emailed users that two licensed insolvency practitioners were appointed joint administrators of Roli on October 20. The company went into administration, the UK process that manages corporate insolvency. This is the second time Roli has gone bankrupt.

That has left a small but bereft community of customers with no word on getting the products they paid for. The Roli community has expressed sadness, anger, or outright confusion. In Facebook groups, the r/Roli subreddit, and other forums, dismayed users have struggled to find recourse for Roli equipment purchases ranging from hundreds to thousands of dollars. The Roli subreddit has been awash with posts from customers who say they paid for orders months or years ago and have received no response or refund since then.

Existing owners also worry about the long-term impact. Roli instruments rely heavily on proprietary software launchers and companion apps to connect, map sounds, and configure settings. While the hardware still functions, users fear that lack of software support will eventually leave their gear bricked.

Roli has not publicly communicated about its future strategy with customers. The company did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment; Lamb did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Roli’s primary financial backers, investment firms TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, also did not respond.

Roli has faced financial struggles before.

The company started in 2009 but really took off after musician Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony’s Innovation Fund in 2018. Musicians like Dream Theater keyboardist Jordan Rudess supported and touted Roli’s gadgets. Ryan Gosling’s character played a Seaboard Grand in the 2016 movie La La Land. In the late 2010s, the tech and the company were hailed as a hit.

That tune changed in 2020. The British government’s Future Fund—a taxpayer-funded relief package issued to help businesses during the pandemic—partially bailed out Roli from a Covid-19-induced financial crisis. Even then, Roli went into administration for the first time in 2021. It survived by relaunching as Luminary Roli and focusing on music-learning devices like the light-up Lumi keyboard and the Airwave, a digital theremin that doubled as an AI piano teacher.

Through all of that, customers have had issues with how the company communicates. Users who ordered the Lumi keyboard found orders unexpectedly delayed, with no indication from the company on what was happening.

“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise, tells WIRED. “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.”

Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims. Every person we spoke with who worked with Lamb compared him to a Steve Jobs-esque character. One person described the experience of being at Roli as being in a movie, where Lamb saw himself as the main character and everyone else as extras or set pieces.

“I love the company, love the culture, love the people—I didn’t love working for him,” the employee said. “Everyone has their story with him. You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.”

In 2021, another former Roli employee, who also asked not to be identified, uploaded files on GitHub that include various notes chronicling Roli as a hostile workplace. One 16-page PDF is titled “Keeping Roland Happy” and includes multiple sections about how to handle interacting with a pathological narcissist. Several former employees independently described what they viewed as Lamb’s narcissistic behavior, describing him as an arrogant visionary.

“Roland is the archetype of a pathological narcissist,” one employee told WIRED. “Unfortunately, that's what he became. Incredibly brittle when challenged, absolutely shameless, quite reckless, incapable of learning or growth, would rather gamble than take any lessons from the previous experience. It was very disheartening to see.”

“The tragedy here is that it was always fundamentally a great company,” another former employee says. “A lot of what made it great was the sort of all-powerful vision of the founder. But that was so obviously the critical flaw.”

Along with other touch-sensitive devices like the Linnstrument and the Sensel Morph, Roli was a key company in the rise of MIDI polyphonic expression (MPE) devices. MPE technology lets players control a note’s pitch and timbre through touch-based movement. Pressing or sliding fingers over the device’s surface produces varying MIDI notes that capture more expressive playing.

While inventive, Roli’s instruments were altogether very niche—a hard product category to build an Apple-sized audience around. Roli certainly tried, partnering with Apple to sell its Roli Blocks in Apple Stores. Alas, the pandemic caused dire supply chain issues, and the company couldn’t keep up with orders. After the pandemic, bankruptcy, and the rebrand, little remained to push the company forward except the founder's will.

“This was one of the leading lights of music technology in the world,” one former employee said. “It was truly an inventing company—the stuff it made had never been made before. So it's a real shame.”

The response to Roli’s collapse hasn’t been pure dismay. After months of delays and frustration, Reddit users have gathered to mourn the company—and to make sure its devices keep working.

Sam Hocking, a UK audio engineer who runs an audio tools company called Demix.me, also owns multiple Roli Seaboard Blocks. Even before Roli went into administration, Hocking had been building software that could keep the equipment working as a capable MIDI device. He shared his vibe-coded configuration tools in the Roli subreddit and on GitHub, so Roli’s Grand, Rise, Airwave, and Block devices can work without the Roli launcher.

Hocking says his Seaboards are nearly 10 years old and still working. Despite the company’s rocky history and poor communication, he still wants to keep his devices. They’re high quality, cost a good chunk of money, and feel somewhat irreplaceable.

He’s not alone. Other users on the subreddit have joined in, adding their own tweaks and fixes to the software that may keep at least a few of these devices alive.

“They're quite a unique product; there's not another keyboard type out there,” Hocking says. “Nobody likes to spend money and then not be able to use it.”

#473. Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Use AI to Vote

As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.

Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.

But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.

Even supposedly nonpartisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.

Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections, and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.

According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that conflated the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.

Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.

Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. Pink slime sites present as mainstream news websites but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.

Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the pink slime sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing pink slime sites in 30 percent of cases.

“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”

#471. Germany's search for a nuclear waste site

Finland has become the first country with a final storage facility for nuclear waste. Germany is still searching for a site, while some countries have yet to start. Costs are expected to total many billions of euros.

Hardly any environmental and political challenge is as complex as the disposal of radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. In almost all of the world's nuclear-powered nations — some 31 countries currently operate or once operated nuclear power plants — the issue remains largely unresolved. This is despite the first large-scale nuclear power plant going online 72 years ago in the Soviet Union.

Finland recently became the first country in the world to approve a repository for radioactive nuclear waste. Located 400 meters (1,300 feet) underground on an island in western Finland, it is situated at the site of one of the country's two nuclear power plants. The project took around 40 years to complete.

Yet in every other country, including Germany, the problem remains unresolved. To make an everyday analogy: The garbage has already been placed outside for collection, but the garbage truck has not yet arrived. There is simply no landfill to take it to. It is not a pleasant sight, yet hardly anyone wants to live near such a site.

Germany has made some progress: The specially established Federal Company for Radioactive Waste Disposal (BGE) has now been searching for a suitable site for almost ten years, one that, like the Finnish repository, would be located deep underground.

Most experts have long agreed on one point: Nuclear waste, especially the spent fuel elements from nuclear power plants, which will remain radioactive for many thousands of years, must be stored underground.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany hopes to identify a site for a final repository by 2050. But that is still a long way off, which is why Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) wants to examine whether the search process can be accelerated.

And, the government says, at least there is a roadmap in place. "Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan have not yet advanced their procedures as far as we have," ministry spokesperson, Stephan Gabriel Haufe, said at a regular government press conference this week. "Finland is certainly the country making the fastest progress worldwide. But Germany is among the leading countries."

This week, the BGE announced that only 5% of Germany's land area, spread across 11 of the country's 16 states, remains under consideration as a potential site for a final repository. The agency is consulting geologists, nuclear experts, and physicists, as well as citizens and politicians. What is already clear, is that the nuclear waste generated during decades of nuclear power production will remain in Germany.

Most of the waste is currently stored at or near the sites where it was generated. These include the 19 former nuclear power plants currently being decommissioned, as well as several research facilities.

In 2011, following the reactor disaster in Fukushima, Japan, Germany decided to phase out the commercial use of nuclear energy, and the last nuclear power plant was shut down in 2023. The waste, however, remains in interim storage.

"It must be shown that a repository will remain safe over a very long period of time," said BGE spokesperson Dagmar Dehmer. "In Finland, that means 100,000 years; in Germany, Switzerland, and France, one million years. But no matter how far into the future scientists project, the effort involved is enormous. It requires a detailed analysis of developments over time, the interactions between geology and technology, and the decay of radionuclides, as well as an assessment of how these factors affect safety."

The procedure is indeed complex: First, potential sites are evaluated for their geological suitability. Will the rock formation remain stable at a depth of 400 meters? Could groundwater become contaminated? The goal is to identify a location where the repository would be surrounded by a rock layer around 100 meters thick, providing a natural barrier. Suitable geological formations include layers of clay, granite, and rock salt.

As the requirements become progressively stricter, fewer and fewer potential sites remain under consideration. Other factors, such as proximity to major cities, come into play only much later in the process. Few communities are likely to welcome a repository for radioactive waste, whether in an urban area or in the countryside.

Building and maintaining trust is also part of Dehmer's job. She often has to explain why it is important to deal with the legacy of the nuclear age, regardless of where people stand on nuclear energy.

Finland has succeeded in doing so, Dehmer believes. "There is a high level of trust in government action in Finland," she said. "The country's supervisory and licensing authority, STUK, is one of its most respected institutions. Germany can learn from Finland by remaining consistent, avoiding frequent changes in direction, and demonstrating the patience needed to achieve a successful outcome."

The disposal of nuclear waste is extremely expensive. Even today, the search for a final repository and the storage of nuclear waste at former reactor sites cost around €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) per year.

Experts estimate that the final repository itself will cost roughly €14 billion ($16.4 billion) once completed. If all goes according to plan, 28,000 cubic meters of radioactive waste will eventually be stored deep underground on a permanent basis.

This article was originally published in German.

#465. Ferrari raises 2026 guidance after Q3 earnings beat

Ferrari on Tuesday raised its 2026 guidance after the sports car maker slightly beat Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.

Here's how Ferrari performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:

Ferrari raised its guidance to revenue of 7.65 billion euros, up from 7.6 billion euros; adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to 3 billion euros, up from 2.97 billion euros; and adjusted EPS to at least 9.85 euros, up from at least 9.68 euros.

The automaker also upgraded its expectations for industrial free cash flow to up to 1.65 billion euros, up from previous expectations for at least 1.55 billion euros.

This is the second consecutive quarter Ferrari has raised its 2026 guidance, despite vehicle shipments being lower by 318 units through the first nine months of the year, at 10,170 vehicles, compared with last year. The decline is led by fewer shipments to the Americas and China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Ferrari said Tuesday that the guidance improvements were a result of stronger-than-expected customer personalizations, lower than anticipated currency headwinds and a second place finish in the Formula 1 championship.

"Our order book now reaches into 2028, and we still have two more launches to come this year. In addition, we continue to create engaging events around the world to further tighten the bonds with our clients and partners across Racing, Sports Cars and Lifestyle," Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said in a release.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Tuesday that Ferrari's results were largely in line with Wall Street expectations. However, he said shares may be "under slight pressure given some were hoping for a bigger guidance raise, but expect it to get better once folks realize these results are healthy."

Ferrari's U.S. stock initially declined on the results before turning positive to close Tuesday at $414.77 a share, up 2.9%.

#461. Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist

For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.

Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.

Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.

“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”

Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.

Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.”

At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes.

Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.”

While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year.

Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post.

If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”
